# Shirakaba

> Shirakaba is a PHP 8.5 web framework: a small, PSR-compliant core with official packages for JSON APIs, databases and an ORM, authentication, OpenAPI, background jobs and real-time events, configured in PHP and checked by PHPStan at level max. It is not in model training data; read these documents instead of assuming another framework's API.

Generated by `composer docs:generate`; do not edit. Every document of shirakaba/docs in full.

---

<!-- index.md -->

# Shirakaba documentation for coding agents

Shirakaba is a PHP 8.5 web framework that is **not in your training data**. Do not guess its
API from Laravel, Symfony, Slim or other frameworks: names and conventions differ, and
several common patterns are deliberately absent. Read the relevant page below before writing
code, and check the class you use in [api.md](api.md).

This documentation matches the installed version of Shirakaba.

## Rules agents most often get wrong

- **Configuration is PHP code.** There are no config files, no service container and no
  autowiring. Dependencies are passed to constructors and closures in a builder function
  ([principles](design/01-principles.md)).
- **Handlers declare what they read.** Parameters carry `#[Path]`, `#[Query]`, `#[Header]`,
  `#[Cookie]`, `#[JsonBody]`, `#[FormBody]` or `#[Db]`; values are parsed strictly and bad
  input is a 400 Problem Details response, never a PHP warning.
- **No global state.** Nothing reads superglobals or static properties; per-request values
  live in the `RequestScope`. Code must be safe in worker runtimes that serve many requests
  per process ([runtimes and scopes](design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md)).
- **GET and HEAD handlers take a `Reader`, never a `Writer`.** PHPStan reports violations
  ([static analysis and agents](design/13-static-analysis-and-agents.md) and [database](design/08-database.md)).
- **Entities are `final readonly` classes.** There is no unit of work, no `save()`, no
  lazy loading: write with `Entities::insert()`, `update()`, `patch()`, `delete()`, and load
  relations with `with(...)->into(Projection::class)` ([database](design/08-database.md)). Change an entity with
  `Entities::change($entity, [...])`.
- **Instants are `DateTimeImmutable` in UTC; dates are `Shirakaba\Time\LocalDate`.** Input must
  be RFC 3339 with an offset. Read the current time from a PSR-20 `ClockInterface`, never
  `time()` or `new DateTimeImmutable()` ([date and time](design/07-date-and-time.md)).
- **Entities with `#[RequiredScope]` need `scoped(...)` on reads and `scopes:` on writes**;
  forgetting it throws `ScopeMissing`.
- **Errors are Problem Details.** Throw `HttpFailure` (or its named constructors) for
  client errors; unexpected exceptions become a bare 500 ([errors and observability](design/05-errors-and-observability.md)).

## Verify your work

Run these before you finish; they are the definition of done in Shirakaba projects:

- `vendor/bin/phpstan analyse` with `shirakaba/phpstan` included (wiring, safe methods, clocks,
  ORM names and types);
- the test suite (`TestClient`, `ConsoleTester`, `StatementLog` for N+1 checks);
- `app openapi --strict` when routes changed;
- `app db:diff --check` and `app db:lint` when entities or migrations changed.

To find out what the application declares instead of guessing, use `app routes`,
`app routes:show <name or "METHOD /path">`, `app entities` and `app entities:show <Entity>`
(add `--json` for structured output), when the application registers them.

Command names depend on how the application registers them; see
[guide/13-command-line.md](guide/13-command-line.md).

<!-- guide/01-getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

Shirakaba needs PHP 8.5. The packages are not on Packagist yet, so add the Shirakaba
repository to the application's `composer.json` first ([principles](../design/01-principles.md)):

```json
"repositories": [{"type": "composer", "url": "https://nazo.github.io/shirakaba/"}]
```

Then install the core and a runtime:

```sh
composer require shirakaba/core shirakaba/runtime-fpm
```

An application is plain PHP. Keep the assembly in one file that returns the `AppBuilder`,
so the web entry point, the tests and tools such as the OpenAPI generator share it:

```php
<?php // app.php

use Shirakaba\Core\AppBuilder;
use Shirakaba\Core\Extraction\Path;
use Shirakaba\Core\Http\Text;

$app = new AppBuilder();
$app->get('/hello/{name}', static fn (#[Path] string $name): Text => new Text('Hello, ' . $name));

return $app;
```

```php
<?php // public/index.php

use Shirakaba\Core\AppBuilder;
use Shirakaba\Runtime\Fpm\FpmRuntime;

require __DIR__ . '/../vendor/autoload.php';

$builder = require __DIR__ . '/../app.php';
assert($builder instanceof AppBuilder);

new FpmRuntime()->run($builder->build(lazy: true));
```

Try it with PHP's built-in server:

```sh
php -S 127.0.0.1:8080 public/index.php
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/hello/world
```

There are no configuration files and nothing is discovered: everything the application
contains is in `app.php`, where PHPStan and your IDE can see it ([principles](../design/01-principles.md)).

`build()` checks every route and handler signature and fails with `InvalidApplication`
before the first request. `build(lazy: true)` postpones those checks to the first request of
each route, which keeps PHP-FPM fast; keep a test that calls `build()` so mistakes are still
caught (see [Testing](09-testing.md)).

---

<!-- guide/02-routing-and-handlers.md -->

# Routing and handlers

## Routes

```php
$app->get('/users', $handlers->list(...));
$app->post('/users', $handlers->create(...));
$app->get('/users/{id}', $handlers->show(...))->name('users.show');
$app->route(['PUT', 'PATCH'], '/users/{id}', $handlers->update(...));
$app->get('/files/{path...}', $files->download(...)); // catch-all, last segment only
```

Groups share a prefix and middleware; `''` is the group's own path:

```php
$app->group('/admin', function (RouteGroup $admin) use ($auth, $handlers): void {
    $admin->middleware($auth);
    $admin->get('', $handlers->dashboard(...));     // /admin
    $admin->get('/stats', $handlers->stats(...));   // /admin/stats
});
```

Matching ([routing and handlers](../design/04-routing-and-handlers.md)):

- static segments beat parameters, parameters beat catch-alls, decided from the left;
- `/users` and `/users/` are different paths;
- an unknown path is a 404, a known path with the wrong method a 405 with `Allow`;
- `HEAD` falls back to `GET` without a body, and `OPTIONS` is answered automatically;
- two routes with the same method and shape are a build error.

## Handlers

A handler is any callable. The recommended style is a class whose constructor takes the
application's services, registered method by method with first-class callables
([principles](../design/01-principles.md)):

```php
final readonly class UserHandlers
{
    public function __construct(private Mailer $mailer) {}

    public function show(#[Path] UserId $id, #[Db] UserQueries $users): Json { ... }
}

$handlers = new UserHandlers($mailer);
$app->get('/users/{id}', $handlers->show(...));
```

Handlers are built once and, under worker runtimes, serve many requests: never store
request data in their properties ([runtimes and scopes](../design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md); `shirakaba/phpstan` checks this).

Every parameter needs an extractor attribute (see [Reading request data](03-request-data.md))
or one of the injected types `ServerRequestInterface` and `RequestScope`. The return type
must be `ResponseInterface` or a `ResponseValue` such as `Text`, `NoContent` or `Json`;
arrays and other objects are never converted automatically.

## Middleware

Any PSR-15 middleware works:

```php
$app->middleware(
    new TrustedProxies(['10.0.0.0/8'], [ForwardedHeader::For, ForwardedHeader::Proto]),
    new Cors(['https://app.example.com']),
);
```

Global middleware runs for every request, including 404s and errors, so it can decorate
error responses. Group and route middleware (`->middleware(...)` on a group or route) run
only for matched routes, outer groups first.

## Request scope

`RequestScope` holds what belongs to one request: values registered by type, cleanup
callbacks, cancellation and an optional deadline ([runtimes and scopes](../design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md)).

```php
public function process(ServerRequestInterface $request, RequestHandlerInterface $handler): ResponseInterface
{
    RequestScope::of($request)->set($this->tenants->resolve($request));

    return $handler->handle($request);
}

public function report(RequestScope $scope): Json
{
    $tenant = $scope->get(Tenant::class);
    $lock = $this->locks->acquire($tenant);
    $scope->defer($lock->release(...)); // runs when the request ends, even after failures
    ...
}
```

<!-- guide/03-request-data.md -->

# Reading request data

Handler parameters say where their value comes from with an attribute ([routing and handlers](../design/04-routing-and-handlers.md)):

```php
public function search(
    #[Path] int $categoryId,
    #[Query] string $q,
    #[Query('per_page')] int $perPage = 20,
    #[Query] ?Sort $sort = null,              // a backed enum
    #[Header('Accept-Language')] string $language = 'en',
    #[Cookie('theme')] string $theme = 'light',
): Json
```

- Supported types are `string`, `int`, `bool`, backed enums, `DateTimeImmutable`,
  `Shirakaba\Time\LocalDate` and `RequestValue` classes, optionally nullable.
- Parsing is strict: `int` rejects `+1`, `01`, `1.0` and overflow; `bool` accepts `true`,
  `false`, `1` and `0`.
- A missing value uses the default; without one it is a 400, even for nullable types.
- A repeated query key or header for a single value is a 400.
- Every failure is a 400 Problem Details response naming the parameter, without echoing
  the value.

## Dates and times

Instants are `DateTimeImmutable` and must be RFC 3339 with an offset
(`2026-11-11T09:30:00+09:00` or `...Z`); without one the request is a 400, never read in
a server timezone. They arrive normalised to UTC. Calendar dates are `LocalDate`
(`2026-11-11`). JSON bodies, `Json` responses and forms use the same rules, responses
write instants in UTC with `Z` and six fractional digits (`2026-11-11T00:30:00.000000Z`),
so they sort in time order as text, and OpenAPI shows `format: date-time` and `date`
([date and time](../design/07-date-and-time.md)).

`#[DateRange(notBefore: '1900-01-01')]` (from `shirakaba/validation`) bounds dates and
instants. Rules relative to now ("in the future") belong in the handler, which can take a
clock.

For "now", take a `Psr\Clock\ClockInterface` (`Shirakaba\Time\SystemClock`, or
`FrozenClock` in tests) rather than calling `time()` or `new DateTimeImmutable()`.

## Constraints

`shirakaba/validation` adds constraint attributes that work on these parameters and on DTO
fields alike:

```php
#[Query] #[Range(min: 1, max: 100)] int $perPage = 20,
#[Query] #[Length(min: 2)] string $q,
#[Query] #[OneOf(['asc', 'desc'])] string $order = 'asc',
```

Available: `Length`, `Range`, `Count`, `Pattern`, `NotBlank`, `OneOf`, `Email`. They also
describe themselves as JSON Schema keywords in OpenAPI documents.

## Value objects

When a rule belongs to a domain type, write it once in a class implementing
`RequestValue`:

```php
final readonly class TaskId implements RequestValue
{
    private function __construct(public int $value) {}

    public static function fromRequestValue(string $value): ?static
    {
        $id = Scalar::int($value);

        return $id !== null && $id >= 1 ? new static($id) : null;
    }

    public static function requestValueType(): Type
    {
        return new ScalarType('int');
    }

    public static function requestValueConstraints(): array
    {
        return [new Range(min: 1)];
    }
}

public function show(#[Path] TaskId $id): Json
```

## Writing your own extractor

An extractor is an attribute implementing `ParameterExtractor`. `plan()` runs once at build
time, validates the parameter, and returns an `ArgumentResolver` used for every request.
Implement `DescribesParameter` too, so OpenAPI can document it. Keep resolvers free of
request state.

---

<!-- guide/04-json-apis.md -->

# JSON APIs

```sh
composer require shirakaba/json shirakaba/validation
```

## Request bodies

```php
final readonly class NewTask
{
    public function __construct(
        #[NotBlank] #[Length(max: 200)]
        public string $title,
        #[Length(max: 2000)]
        public string $description = '',
        #[ListOf('string')] #[Count(max: 10)]
        public array $tags = [],
    ) {}
}

public function create(#[JsonBody] NewTask $input): Json
```

The DTO's constructor defines the accepted fields ([JSON and OpenAPI](../design/06-json-and-openapi.md)): scalar types, backed enums,
nested DTOs, arrays with `#[ListOf(...)]`, and objects with arbitrary keys with
`#[MapOf(...)]` (`#[MapOf('int')] array $reactions` is `{"👍": 2}`; `Json` writes `{}` when
it is empty, and OpenAPI uses `additionalProperties`). Unknown fields are rejected unless
`#[JsonBody(allowUnknownFields: true)]`; `#[JsonName('per_page')]` renames a field.

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| 415 | `Content-Type` is not JSON |
| 413 | the body exceeds `maxBytes` (1 MiB by default) or has more than `maxMembers` object members (10,000) |
| 400 | malformed JSON, or fields of the wrong type, missing or unknown |
| 422 | a constraint failed |

Field errors are listed in the Problem Details member `errors` with JSON Pointers.

### Partial updates

Use `Optional` where "not sent" differs from "null" or a default:

```php
final readonly class TaskPatch
{
    public function __construct(
        #[OptionalOf('string')] #[NotBlank]
        public Optional $title = new Optional(),
        #[OptionalOf(TaskStatus::class)]
        public Optional $status = new Optional(),
    ) {}
}

$updated = new Task($task->id, $patch->title->or($task->title), ...);
```

## Responses

Mark response DTOs `#[JsonDto]` and `Json` encodes them from their constructor fields, the
same fields OpenAPI describes ([JSON and OpenAPI](../design/06-json-and-openapi.md)):

```php
#[JsonDto]
final readonly class Task
{
    public function __construct(public int $id, public string $title, public TaskStatus $status) {}
}

#[JsonResponse(201, Task::class)]
#[Responds(409, 'A task with this title exists.')]
public function create(#[JsonBody] NewTask $input, #[Db] TaskCommands $tasks): Json
{
    $task = $tasks->add($input->title);

    return new Json($task, headers: ['Location' => '/tasks/' . $task->id]); // 201 from the declaration
}
```

`Json` also accepts arrays, scalars, backed enums and `JsonSerializable` objects. Any other
object is refused with a 500, so entities holding secrets are never serialised by accident.
When a route declares exactly one success status, `Json` uses it by default; returning a
different success status fails an assertion in development.

## Tagged unions

When one endpoint returns several shapes, declare them as a tagged union on the type they
share ([JSON and OpenAPI](../design/06-json-and-openapi.md)). The attribute maps each discriminator value to a `#[JsonDto]` member:

```php
#[JsonUnion('type', [
    'follow' => FollowNotification::class,
    'reaction' => ReactionNotification::class,
])]
interface Notification {}

#[JsonDto]
final readonly class FollowNotification implements Notification
{
    public function __construct(public string $id, public UserSummary $user) {}
}

#[JsonDto]
final readonly class ReactionNotification implements Notification
{
    public function __construct(public string $id, public UserSummary $user, public string $reaction) {}
}

#[JsonResponse(200, Notification::class, list: true)]
public function list(): Json { /* ... */ }
```

`Json` writes each member with its discriminator first (`{"type":"follow","id":...}`), so
members do not declare a `type` field themselves; the build fails if one does. OpenAPI
describes the union as `oneOf` its members with a `discriminator` and mapping, and each
member's `type` as a `const`, so generated clients can narrow on it.

The same union works as a `#[JsonBody]`, a `#[ListOf]` item, a nullable field, an ORM
`#[Json]` column and with `JsonMapper::decode()`: the discriminator picks the member class,
and a missing or unknown value is a 400 pointing at `/type`.

---

<!-- guide/05-forms-and-uploads.md -->

# Forms and uploads

```sh
composer require shirakaba/form
```

```php
final readonly class SignUp
{
    public function __construct(
        #[Email] public string $email,
        public bool $newsletter = false,              // a checkbox: "on" or absent
        #[FormList('string')] public array $interests = [], // interests[]=...
        #[MaxFileSize(2 * 1024 * 1024)] #[FileTypes(['image/png', 'image/jpeg'])]
        public ?UploadedFileInterface $avatar = null,
    ) {}
}

public function signUp(#[FormBody] SignUp $form): Json
```

- Both `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and `multipart/form-data` are accepted.
  URL-encoded bodies are parsed from the raw body, so keys are not renamed as in `$_POST`.
- An empty string is null for nullable non-string fields.
- `FileTypes` checks the type detected from the content; the type the client claims is
  never trusted.
- Files over PHP's upload limit are a 413; other upload errors are field errors.
- URL-encoded bodies over `maxBytes` (1 MiB) or `maxFields` (1,000) are a 413.
- Move accepted files with `$form->avatar->moveTo($path)`. Under FrankenPHP, RoadRunner and
  Swoole, uploads the application did not move are deleted after the request.

Errors use the same format as JSON bodies.

---

<!-- guide/06-database.md -->

# Databases

```sh
composer require shirakaba/database-bridge
```

`shirakaba/database-bridge` connects the database packages to the framework and installs
them: `shirakaba/database` (connections), `shirakaba/query` (the query builder),
`shirakaba/orm` and `shirakaba/migrations`. The packages themselves do not depend on the
framework and work on their own; see [Without the framework](#without-the-framework).

PHP needs the PDO driver for your database: `pdo_mysql`, `pdo_pgsql` (built against
libpq) or `pdo_sqlite`. Check with `php -m | grep -i pdo`.

```php
use Shirakaba\Database\Database;
use Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\DatabaseMiddleware;

$database = new Database(static fn (): PDO => PDO::connect($dsn, $user, $password));
$app->middleware(new DatabaseMiddleware($database));
```

Connections are leased on first use and released with the request scope; a transaction left
open is rolled back ([runtimes and scopes](../design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md)). `DatabaseMiddleware` also answers the ORM's errors:
`EntityNotFound` becomes a 404 and `StaleEntity` a 409.

## Queries and commands

Data access classes take a `Reader` or a `Writer` in their constructor, and handlers ask for
them with `#[Db]`; they are built for each request ([database](../design/08-database.md)):

```php
final readonly class TaskQueries
{
    public function __construct(private Reader $db) {}

    public function find(int $id): ?Task { ... $this->db->fetchOne(...) ... }
}

final readonly class TaskCommands
{
    public function __construct(private Writer $db) {}

    public function add(string $title): Task { ... $this->db->execute(...) ... }
}

public function show(#[Path] TaskId $id, #[Db] TaskQueries $tasks): Json
public function create(#[JsonBody] NewTask $input, #[Db] TaskCommands $tasks): Json
```

`Writer` can read too, and offers `transaction(fn (Writer $db) => ...)`. A transaction
inside another runs in a savepoint, so an inner failure undoes only the inner work.
`transaction($work, retries: 2)` reruns an outermost transaction that hit a deadlock or
serialisation failure; `$work` must then be safe to repeat.

The constructor's other parameters take application services, such as a clock, a storage
client or a `Publisher`, by type from the request scope. Put them there once with the
`Provide` middleware ([database](../design/08-database.md)); a parameter with a default may be left unprovided:

```php
final readonly class NoteCommands
{
    public function __construct(private Writer $db, private ClockInterface $clock, private Publisher $publisher) {}
}

$app->middleware(new Provide([ClockInterface::class => $clock, Publisher::class => $pubsub]));
```

The split documents which handlers write, and `shirakaba/phpstan` enforces it: a GET or HEAD
handler that takes a `Writer`, or a class built from one, is reported ([static analysis and agents](../design/13-static-analysis-and-agents.md)).

### Several databases and replicas

Name further databases in the middleware and select them with `#[Db('name')]`; each database
leases its own connection per request ([database](../design/08-database.md)):

```php
$app->middleware(new DatabaseMiddleware($main, ['analytics' => $analytics]));

public function report(#[Db] OrderQueries $orders, #[Db('analytics')] Reader $events): Json
```

Give a database a read replica, and readers of GET and HEAD requests use it; other requests,
and every Writer, use the primary. A request that has taken a Writer reads from the primary
from then on, so it sees its own writes:

```php
$main = new Database($connectPrimary, reuse: true, replica: new Database($connectReplica, reuse: true));

public function show(#[Path] int $id, #[Db] TaskQueries $tasks): Json                    // replica
public function balance(#[Db(primary: true)] AccountQueries $accounts): Json            // primary
```

Replicas lag behind the primary, so a GET right after a POST from the same client may not
see the POST's data yet; read with `#[Db(primary: true)]` where that matters. Outside handlers,
`RequestDatabase::replicaReader($database, $scope)` makes the same choice and
`RequestDatabase::reader($database, $scope)` always uses the primary.

## Dialects and errors

MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite are supported; the dialect is detected from the driver and
configures each connection: exceptions, native prepared statements, UTC session time
zone, strict SQL mode and `utf8mb4` on MySQL, foreign keys on SQLite. `$db->dialect()`
quotes identifiers and builds `LIMIT` and upsert clauses.

Parameters may be scalars, `null`, backed enums, `DateTimeImmutable` (written in UTC) and
`LocalDate` ([date and time](../design/07-date-and-time.md)). Driver errors become typed exceptions, the same on every database:

```php
try {
    $db->execute('INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES (?)', [$email]);
} catch (UniqueViolation) {
    throw HttpFailure::conflict('The e-mail address is already registered.');
}
```

`UniqueViolation`, `ForeignKeyViolation`, `NotNullViolation`, `TransientFailure`,
`QueryTimedOut` and `ConnectionLost` extend `DatabaseError`.

`$db->withTimeout($seconds)` returns the same Reader or Writer with a time limit for each
statement: PostgreSQL cancels any statement (`statement_timeout`), MySQL a SELECT
(`max_execution_time`), and both raise `QueryTimedOut`. The connection sets the limit only
when it changes, so statements with the same limit share one `SET`, and the next statement
without a limit resets it; a limit never applies to a statement that did not ask for it, and
never outlives the request on a reused connection. SQLite has no such limit and runs the
statement to completion. Bound searches that may scan a whole table:

```php
try {
    $notes = Entities::query(Note::class)->whereColumns(...)->limit(20)->fetch($db->withTimeout(0.5));
} catch (QueryTimedOut) {
    throw new HttpFailure(503, 'The search took too long; try a longer search term.');
}
```

Code that holds the request scope but is not a handler (an authenticator, a job handler)
uses the same per-request connection through `RequestDatabase`:
`RequestDatabase::writer($database, $scope)`. Outside a request (scripts, migrations, tests),
`$database->connect()` opens a connection the caller owns: `$database->connect()->writer()`.

Instants are stored in UTC: use `timestamptz(6)` on PostgreSQL, `DATETIME(6)` on MySQL and
text on SQLite, which Shirakaba writes as `2026-11-11T00:30:00.000000Z` so it sorts in time
order. Columns that already hold local times are not converted automatically; read them
with a `ColumnType` that names their timezone.

MySQL ignores `REFERENCES` written on a column; declare foreign keys as table constraints
(`FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES parents (id)`).

## Query builder

`shirakaba/query` builds SQL from immutable values. Reads run with a `Reader`, writes need a
`Writer`, so the safe-method rule still applies:

```php
$tasks = Select::from('tasks')
    ->columns('id', 'title', 'done', 'created_at')
    ->where('done', '=', false)
    ->whereGroup(fn (Conditions $c) => $c->where('priority', '>', 3)->orWhereNull('due_on'))
    ->orderBy('created_at', 'desc')
    ->limit(20)
    ->fetchInto(TaskSummary::class, $reader);   // list<TaskSummary>

$id = Insert::into('tasks')->values(['title' => $title, 'done' => false])->executeAndGetId($writer);
Update::table('tasks')->set(['done' => true])->where('id', '=', $id)->execute($writer);
Delete::from('tasks')->where('id', '=', $id)->execute($writer);
```

- Names are plain identifiers (`column`, `table.column`); anything else is rejected, so a
  sort column taken from a request cannot inject SQL. Expressions use
  `Sql::raw('LOWER(email) = ?', [$email])`; every value is a bound parameter.
- `whereIn('id', [])` is valid and matches nothing.
- `UPDATE` and `DELETE` without `WHERE` throw unless you call `everyRow()`.
- `fetchInto()` maps rows through the constructor: columns match parameter names or their
  snake_case form, and values are converted to `int`, `float`, `bool`, enums,
  `DateTimeImmutable` (UTC) and `LocalDate`.
- `onConflict(['email'], ['name'])` writes an upsert for each database, and
  `onConflict(['note_id', 'reaction'], ['count' => Sql::raw('reaction_counts.count + 1')])`
  sets a column to an expression, where `<table>.<column>` is the stored row and
  `excluded.<column>` the inserted one; `returning()`
  works on PostgreSQL and SQLite, and `executeAndGetId()` everywhere.
- `after(['id' => $lastId])` pages by key instead of `OFFSET`; `iterate()` streams rows;
  `forUpdate()` locks rows (left out on SQLite, which has no row locks).
- `toSql($dialect)` returns the SQL and parameters for tests and debugging.

## Entities

`shirakaba/orm` maps plain readonly classes to tables ([database](../design/08-database.md)). There is no unit of work:
reads return immutable entities, and each write is one statement you ask for.

```php
#[Table('posts')]
#[BelongsTo('author', Author::class, 'authorId')]
#[HasMany('comments', Comment::class, 'postId', orderBy: 'id')]
#[ManyToMany('files', DriveFile::class, through: 'note_files', localKey: 'note_id', foreignKey: 'file_id', orderBy: 'position')]
final readonly class Post
{
    public function __construct(
        public AuthorId $authorId,                  // single-value classes map to their value
        public string $title,
        public PostStatus $status = PostStatus::Draft,
        public ?LocalDate $publishedOn = null,
        #[Json] public array $meta = [],
        #[CreatedAt] public ?DateTimeImmutable $createdAt = null,
        #[Version] public int $version = 0,
        #[Id, Generated] public ?int $id = null,
    ) {}
}

$post = Entities::insert(new Post($authorId, 'Hello'), $writer);      // id, createdAt, version filled
$post = Entities::get(Post::class, $id, $reader);                      // 404 when missing
$posts = Entities::query(Post::class)->where('status', '=', PostStatus::Published)->orderBy('id')->fetch($reader);
$post = Entities::update(Entities::change($post, ['title' => 'Hi']), $writer); // 409 if stale
Entities::patch(Post::class, $id, ['status' => PostStatus::Draft], $writer);   // named columns only
Entities::delete($post, $writer);
```

Generated keys, timestamps and versions are nullable or defaulted, because a new entity
has none yet. PHP requires parameters with defaults to come after those without, so they
sit at the end of the constructor, and `new Post($authorId, 'Hello')` leaves them out.
Named arguments (`new Post(title: 'Hello', authorId: $authorId)`) read well when the
order matters less than the names.

`#[Version]` starts at 1 on insert, whatever the property's default, and grows with every
`update()`, `patch()` and bulk update. `#[Table('todos', label: 'Todo')]` names the entity
in API errors ("The Todo was not found."); without a label they say "resource" and never
show the class name.

Bulk changes go through a query and keep the managed columns right: versions increase,
`#[UpdatedAt]` is set, scopes and soft deletes apply.

```php
Entities::query(Todo::class)->where('completed', '=', false)->update(['completed' => true], $writer);
Entities::query(Todo::class)->where('completed', '=', true)->delete($writer);
```

Return entities from APIs through a response DTO or a projection, not as they are.
Generated keys and timestamps are nullable in the entity so new ones can omit them, which
is the wrong type for a response, and renaming an entity class would rename the API type.
Response schemas (`#[JsonResponse]`) list every field as required, because every field is
written; `#[JsonDto(name: 'Todo')]` fixes the public schema name independently of the class.

A response DTO needs no mapping code. Its constructor parameters take the entity
properties of the same names, so it declares `int $id` where the entity has `?int $id`,
and a null (an entity that was never inserted) fails instead of reaching the client.
`into()` fills it from a query, `Entities::into()` from an entity in hand, such as the
result of `insert()` or `update()`:

```php
#[JsonDto(name: 'Todo')]
final readonly class TodoView
{
    public function __construct(
        public int $id,
        public string $title,
        public bool $completed,
        public DateTimeImmutable $createdAt,
    ) {}
}

$views = Entities::query(Todo::class)->orderBy('id')->into(TodoView::class, $reader);
$view = Entities::into(Entities::insert(new Todo('Write docs'), $writer), TodoView::class);
return new Json($view, headers: ['Location' => '/todos/' . $view->id]);   // $view->id is an int
```

Each parameter must name an entity property (with the same or a wider type), a requested
relation or the entity itself, so a typo fails before any query runs, and the
`shirakaba/phpstan` rule reports it during analysis. `examples/tasks` shows entities, response
DTOs, optimistic locking and a bulk update in a small API.

Columns are the snake_case property names unless `#[Column('name')]` says otherwise;
`#[Embedded]` spreads a value object over prefixed columns; `#[Column(type: ...)]` takes a
`ColumnType` for anything else.

Relations are declared on the class but never loaded on access. Ask for them and read the
result into a projection, a class with the entity (or its properties by name) and one
parameter per relation:

```php
final readonly class PostView
{
    /** @param list<CommentView> $comments */
    public function __construct(
        public Post $post,
        public Author $author,
        #[Items(CommentView::class)] public array $comments,   // CommentView(Comment $comment, Author $author)
    ) {}
}

$views = Entities::query(Post::class)->with('author', 'comments.author')->into(PostView::class, $reader);
```

`withWhere('comments', fn (EntityQuery $c) => $c->where('approved', '=', true))` filters or
orders the loaded rows; `withCount('comments')` fills an `int $commentsCount` parameter
with one grouped query. `#[Json]` also stores a DTO, mapped with `shirakaba/json`'s rules.

A response DTO can be the projection itself. `#[From('notifier')] UserView $user` takes a
property, relation or count of another name, and `#[Computed]` parameters take values the
entity does not have, such as counts from a separate query. The callback receives all
loaded entities, so one query serves the page, and returns the values by index:

```php
$views = Entities::query(Note::class)->with('user')->into(NoteView::class, $reader,
    static function (array $notes) use ($reactionCounts, $reader): array {
        $reactions = $reactionCounts->forNotes(array_map(static fn (Note $n): int => $n->id, $notes), $reader);

        return array_map(static fn (Note $n): array => ['reactions' => $reactions[$n->id] ?? []], $notes);
    });
```

`Entities::into($note, NoteView::class, ['reactions' => $counts])` does the same for one
entity. A computed parameter with a default may be left out.

Nested projections can have `#[Computed]` parameters too, such as the reply inside a note
view. The callback then receives those related entities as a second list; return their values
after the query's, so one query still serves every level:

```php
static function (array $notes, array $related) use ($reactionCounts, $reader): array {
    $all = [...$notes, ...$related];
    $reactions = $reactionCounts->forNotes(array_map(static fn (Note $n): int => $n->id, $all), $reader);

    return array_map(static fn (Note $n): array => ['reactions' => $reactions[$n->id] ?? []], $all);
}
```

Each relation level is one `WHERE … IN (…)` query, and belongs-to and many-to-many relations
at the end of a path share their queries across paths (one join-table read per relation, one
read per entity class), so this runs three statements (posts, comments,
authors) however many posts there are. A relation filtered with `withWhere()` keeps its own
query. A projection whose parameters do not match the requested relations
is rejected before any query runs. `whereHas('comments', fn ($c) => $c->where('approved',
'=', true))` filters by relations with `EXISTS`.

Conditions on an entity's properties are joined with AND. For OR, group them; names and values
are mapped as in `where()`, groups nest, and `whereNotIn()` excludes values or a subquery's results:

```php
// Own notes, or public notes of the people I follow.
Entities::query(Note::class)
    ->whereGroup(fn (PropertyConditions $c) => $c
        ->where('userId', '=', $me)
        ->orWhereGroup(fn (PropertyConditions $g) => $g
            ->whereIn('userId', $followed)
            ->where('visibility', '=', Visibility::Public)))
    ->fetch($db);
```

### Scopes and soft deletes

Filters that must apply to every query of an entity are scopes. A `#[RequiredScope]`
must be passed by each query, so a forgotten tenant fails instead of leaking rows; a
`#[DefaultScope]` always applies:

```php
#[Table('projects')]
#[RequiredScope(InTenant::class)]
#[SoftDelete]                                   // delete() sets deletedAt; queries skip such rows
final readonly class Project { /* ... public ?DateTimeImmutable $deletedAt = null ... */ }

Entities::query(Project::class)->scoped(new InTenant($tenantId))->fetch($reader);
Entities::get(Project::class, $id, $reader, [new InTenant($tenantId)]);
Entities::query(Project::class)->scoped($tenant)->withoutScope(NotDeleted::class)->fetch($reader); // include deleted
```

Scopes also apply to related entities loaded with `with()`, to `whereHas()`, and to writes
by key: `Entities::update($project, $writer, scopes: [$tenant])` (likewise `patch()`,
`delete()`, `restore()`, `forceDelete()`) touches the row only inside the scope, so a forged
key cannot reach another tenant's row. `upsert()` refuses entities with required scopes. They are
switched off one by one with `withoutScope()`; there is no way to switch off all of them.
`Entities::restore()` and `Entities::forceDelete()` undo or complete a soft delete.

### Multi-tenant applications

Give every tenant-owned entity a required scope, and let the scope also check inserts, so a
forged tenant id is refused:

```php
final readonly class InOrganization implements Scope, ScopeOnInsert
{
    public function __construct(private string $organizationId) {}

    public function apply(EntityQuery $query): EntityQuery
    {
        return $query->where('organizationId', '=', $this->organizationId);
    }

    public function admits(object $entity): bool
    {
        return $entity->organizationId === $this->organizationId;
    }
}

#[Table('boards')]
#[RequiredScope(InOrganization::class)]
final readonly class Board { ... public string $organizationId ... }

Entities::insert($board, $writer, scopes: [$org]);              // ScopeViolation for another organization
Entities::load($boards, 'cards', $reader, [$org]);              // relations take the scope too
```

A table without its own tenant column is scoped through its parent: the scope's `apply()`
calls `whereHas('board', ...)`. Data access classes that take the organization once keep the
handlers short; put the scope in them with `Provide` ([database](../design/08-database.md)).

`shirakaba/phpstan` reports a query of a scoped entity that cannot have the scope: a chain from
`Entities::query()` that is executed without `scoped()` or `withoutScope()`, and
`Entities::find()`, `get()`, `update()`, `patch()`, `delete()`, `restore()`, `forceDelete()`,
`insert()`, `insertAll()` or `load()` without it in `$scopes`. Queries built across functions
are left to `ScopeMissing` at run time, so keep a test that reads as another tenant.

On PostgreSQL, row-level security adds a second line of defence that also covers raw queries
([database](../design/08-database.md)). Set the tenant on the request's connection right after authentication:

```sql
ALTER TABLE boards ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY boards_tenant ON boards
    USING (organization_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.organization_id', true), '')::uuid);
```

```php
final readonly class TenantSetting implements MiddlewareInterface
{
    public function __construct(private Database $database) {}

    public function process(ServerRequestInterface $request, RequestHandlerInterface $handler): ResponseInterface
    {
        $scope = RequestScope::of($request);
        $user = $scope->find(User::class);
        if ($user !== null) {
            RequestDatabase::setting($this->database, $scope, 'app.organization_id', $user->organizationId);
        }

        return $handler->handle($request);
    }
}
```

The setting applies to every statement of the request, is set again after a rollback, and is
cleared before the connection serves another request. RLS binds only roles that do not own
the table (or tables with `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`) and are not superusers, so connect as
an application role; a pooler in transaction mode (PgBouncer) breaks session settings.
MySQL and SQLite have no RLS, and `setting()` refuses there.

## Caching query results

Nothing is cached unless you ask. `shirakaba/query-cache` caches chosen reads in any PSR-16
cache, tagged with the tables they read:

```php
$cache = new QueryCache($psr16, 'shop');   // application-scoped; the namespace names the database

$countries = $cache->fetchInto(Country::class, Select::from('countries')->orderBy('name'), $reader, ttl: 3600);
$cache->execute(Update::table('countries')->set(['name' => $name])->where('code', '=', $code), $writer);
$cache->invalidate($writer, 'pricing');   // a custom tag
```

Writes through `execute()` and `invalidate()` retire tags after the transaction commits;
a rolled-back write retires nothing (`Writer::afterCommit()` is available for your own
side effects). Entries are JSON, never `serialize()`, and hits and misses appear in the
access log and traces as `db.cache.hit` and `db.cache.miss`.

## Migrations

`shirakaba/migrations` applies versioned schema changes written in PHP. List them in order;
the keys are permanent IDs:

```php
final readonly class CreateTasks implements Reversible
{
    public function up(Schema $schema): void
    {
        $schema->create('tasks', static function (Blueprint $table): void {
            $table->id();
            $table->bigInteger('owner_id');
            $table->string('title', 200);
            $table->boolean('done')->default(false);
            $table->instant('created_at');
            $table->date('due_on')->nullable();
            $table->string('code', 16)->bytewise();     // binary collation: case-sensitive, byte order
            $table->foreign('owner_id')->references('users')->onDelete('cascade');
            $table->index(['owner_id', 'done']);
        });
    }

    public function down(Schema $schema): void
    {
        $schema->drop('tasks');
    }
}

// migrations.php, for the CLI
return new Migrations($database, ['2026_11_11_create_tasks' => new CreateTasks()]);
```

```sh
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate status --config=migrations.php
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate migrate --config=migrations.php --dry-run   # print the SQL
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate migrate --config=migrations.php
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate rollback --config=migrations.php --steps=1
```

- Column types follow [date and time](../design/07-date-and-time.md): `instant()` stores UTC with microseconds, `date()` a
  `LocalDate`, `json()` is `JSONB` on PostgreSQL.
- Foreign keys are table constraints, which MySQL requires. SQLite cannot add one to an
  existing table.
- On PostgreSQL and SQLite each migration runs in a transaction. MySQL commits DDL
  implicitly, so a migration that fails halfway there needs repair by hand; keep MySQL
  migrations to one change each.
- An advisory lock on MySQL and PostgreSQL keeps two deployments from migrating at once.

Indexes are built with `index()`, `unique()` and `expressionIndex()`, and take an index
method, a PostgreSQL operator class and, for an expression, a statistics target. A substring
search such as `LIKE '%term%'` needs a trigram index on PostgreSQL:

```php
public function up(Schema $schema): void
{
    $schema->extension('pg_trgm');
    $schema->alter('notes', static function (Blueprint $table): void {
        $table->expressionIndex('notes_search', "lower(coalesce(cw, '') || ' ' || coalesce(text, ''))")
            ->using('gin')->operatorClass('gin_trgm_ops')->statistics(1000);
    });
}
```

Queries must use the same expression to use the index (`whereColumns()` with `Sql::raw()`).
The statistics target matters for text: at the default of 100, PostgreSQL may take a rare word
for a common one and scan the table in key order instead. The expression is SQL as written for
the database at hand (MySQL concatenates with `CONCAT`, not `||`), and what a database cannot
express (GIN on MySQL, operator classes outside PostgreSQL) fails when the migration is built.
Searches whose pattern is too short for trigrams still scan; bound them with `withTimeout()`.

After migrating, `SchemaCheck::entities([Task::class, ...], $reader)` lists entity
properties whose columns are missing or nullable when the property is not, for a CI step.

```sh
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate lint --config=migrations.php            # risky changes in pending migrations
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate diff --config=migrations.php --class=AddDueDates --namespace='App\Migrations'
vendor/bin/shirakaba-migrate diff --config=migrations.php --check   # exits with 1 when a migration is missing
```

`lint` warns about dropped tables and columns, renames, NOT NULL columns without a
default, and indexes or foreign keys added to existing tables, and exits with 1, so CI can
stop a deployment. `diff` prints a migration for the tables, join tables, foreign keys and
columns the entities listed in `new Migrations($db, [...], entities: [...])` need. It
never drops or changes anything, so review it and add indexes before committing it.

## Without the framework

`shirakaba/database`, `shirakaba/query`, `shirakaba/query-cache`, `shirakaba/migrations` and
`shirakaba/orm` require no framework package ([database](../design/08-database.md)), so a script, a worker or an
application on another framework can use them alone:

```sh
composer require shirakaba/orm
```

```php
$database = new Database(static fn (): PDO => PDO::connect($dsn, $user, $password), reuse: true);

$lease = $database->lease();                    // borrow a pooled connection
try {
    $notes = Entities::query(Note::class)->where('done', '=', false)->fetch($lease->connection->reader());
} finally {
    $lease->release();                          // roll back what is open, reset, return to the pool
}
```

`lease()` takes an optional `EventSink`, which receives a `ConnectionLeased` and then a
`StatementExecuted` for every statement (`DatabaseEvent`s with a name, a duration and
attributes); the bridge passes one that reports them to the request's observers.
`#[Json]` columns holding arrays need nothing more; columns holding a DTO need
`shirakaba/json`. The commands (`EntityCommands`, `MigrationCommands`, `shirakaba-migrate`)
and the 404/409 answers for entity errors come with the bridge.

---

<!-- guide/07-authentication-and-sessions.md -->

# Authentication, sessions and CSRF

## Bearer tokens and JWT

```sh
composer require shirakaba/auth
```

```php
$verifier = new JwtVerifier(
    [JwtKey::rsa($publicKeyPem, 'key-2026')],
    static fn (array $claims, RequestScope $scope): ?User => new Users(RequestDatabase::reader($scope->get(Database::class), $scope))->find($claims['sub'] ?? ''),
    issuer: 'https://auth.example.com',
    audience: 'api',
);
$app->middleware(new BearerAuthentication($verifier));

public function me(#[Authenticated] User $user): Json      // 401 without a valid token
public function feed(#[Authenticated] ?User $user): Json   // optional authentication
```

`JwtVerifier` supports HS256, RS256 and ES256. The algorithm comes from the key, never
from the token; `exp` is required; issuer and audience are checked when configured
([security](../design/09-security.md)). For anything else, implement `TokenVerifier`. It is built once with the
application and receives each request's scope, so a verifier for opaque tokens stored in
the database reads them through the request's connection; add it after
`DatabaseMiddleware`:

```php
final readonly class StoredTokens implements TokenVerifier
{
    public function verify(string $token, RequestScope $scope): ?object
    {
        $row = Entities::query(AccessToken::class)
            ->where('tokenHash', '=', hash('sha256', $token))
            ->first(RequestDatabase::reader($scope->get(Database::class), $scope));

        return $row === null ? null : new Viewer($row->userId);
    }
}

$app->middleware(new DatabaseMiddleware($database), new BearerAuthentication(new StoredTokens()));
```

Middleware that authenticates in its own way can answer 401 with the same header through
`BearerAuthentication::challenge('api', 'invalid_token')`.

## Sessions and CSRF

```sh
composer require shirakaba/session
```

```php
$app->middleware(
    new SessionMiddleware(new FileSessionStore('/var/lib/app/sessions')),
    new CsrfProtection(['https://app.example.com']),
);

public function login(RequestScope $scope, #[FormBody] Login $form): Response
{
    $session = Session::of($scope);
    $session->regenerate();               // prevents session fixation
    $session->set('user', $user->id);
    $session->flash('notice', 'Welcome back');
    ...
}
```

`regenerate()` at login and `invalidate()` at logout also replace the CSRF token, so a
token seen before the change no longer works; forms rendered before it must be reloaded.

Pick the store by how the application runs:

| Store | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `DatabaseSessionStore` (`shirakaba/session-database`) | several instances behind a load balancer, containers with a read-only root filesystem |
| `RedisSessionStore` (`shirakaba/session-redis`) | the same, when Redis (or Valkey, ElastiCache) is at hand; Redis expires sessions itself |
| `FileSessionStore` | one server with a writable, persistent directory |
| `InMemorySessionStore` | tests, or a single worker process |

```php
$app->middleware(new SessionMiddleware(new DatabaseSessionStore($database)), new CsrfProtection([...]));

// migrations: '2026_11_18_create_sessions' => new CreateSessionsTable(),
// a scheduled job: $store->prune($writer);
```

`RedisSessionStore` takes a `RedisClient` (`shirakaba/redis`, `RedisClient::fromUrl('rediss://user:password@host:6379/0')`)
and answers 503 when Redis cannot be reached rather than starting an empty session.

`DatabaseSessionStore` keys rows by the SHA-256 hash of the session ID, so reading the table
does not hand out live sessions, and saves outside transactions on the request's connection,
so a request that rolls back keeps its session. Expired rows are never loaded; `prune()`
deletes them.

`FileSessionStore` writes files readable only by their owner. Expired sessions that are
never read again stay on disk until `collectGarbage()` runs, so call it from a scheduled
job.

A store of your own implements `SessionStore`; each call receives the request scope.
`SessionStoreChecks::run($store, $clock, $scope)` returns what it gets wrong (expiry,
replacing, deleting, keeping sessions apart), for a test.

Sessions live in the request scope and never use PHP's `session_*` functions, so they are
safe under worker runtimes. Cookies default to `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Lax`.
`CsrfProtection` rejects cross-site state changes using `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `Origin`, and
falls back to a token from `CsrfProtection::token($session)` in a `_csrf` field or an
`X-CSRF-Token` header.

---

<!-- guide/08-errors-and-observability.md -->

# Errors, logging and tracing

## Errors

Throw `HttpFailure` for errors meant for clients:

```php
throw HttpFailure::notFound(sprintf('Task %d does not exist.', $id));
throw HttpFailure::unauthorized('Bearer realm="api"');
throw new HttpFailure(409, 'Already archived.', type: 'https://example.com/problems/archived');
```

They become RFC 9457 Problem Details (`application/problem+json`). Any other exception is
a bare 500 whose body never contains the message ([errors and observability](../design/05-errors-and-observability.md)). Replace the format, for
example with HTML pages, through `$app->renderErrorsWith($renderer)`; required headers such
as `Allow` and `WWW-Authenticate` are kept whatever the renderer does.

Libraries that do not know HTTP throw their own exceptions. A `TranslatesFailures` turns
them into failures: register one with `$app->translateFailures($translator)`, or let global
middleware implement it, as `DatabaseMiddleware` does to answer the ORM's `EntityNotFound`
with a 404 and `StaleEntity` with a 409 ([database](../design/08-database.md)). What a translator returns is shown to
clients, so pass on only messages written for them.

Problems Shirakaba produces itself carry a stable `code` (`invalid-body`, `missing-parameter`,
...), and each entry of `errors` has one too (`required`, `unknown-field`,
`invalid-date-time`, ...), so clients and tests can branch without parsing the English
`detail`. The codes are constants of `ProblemCode`, each explained in
`vendor/shirakaba/docs/problems/`. Give your own failures a code the same way:
`new HttpFailure(409, 'Already archived.', extensions: ['code' => 'already-archived'])`.

## Logging

Because 500 responses are bare, production needs an observer that records the cause:

```sh
composer require shirakaba/log
```

```php
$app->observe(new LoggingObserver(new StreamLogger(), accessLog: true));
```

Unexpected errors are logged at `error` with the exception, client errors at `debug`,
cleanup failures at `warning`. Access lines use the route template, never the raw path.
`StreamLogger` writes JSON lines to standard error; any PSR-3 logger works.

## Tracing

```sh
composer require shirakaba/opentelemetry open-telemetry/sdk
```

```php
$app->observe(new TracingObserver($tracerProvider->getTracer('my-api')));
```

One server span per request, named after the route (`GET /tasks/{id}`), continuing the
caller's `traceparent`; only 5xx responses mark it as an error ([errors and observability](../design/05-errors-and-observability.md)).

Observers combine: `$app->observe(new LoggingObserver($logger), new TracingObserver($tracer))`.
A failing observer never affects the response or the other observers.

## Database statements

With `shirakaba/database`, every statement a request runs is reported to observers: the
access log line ends with `db.statement=3` and carries the count and total time, and the
request span gets one `db.statement` event per statement (with `db.query.text`, never the
parameter values) and `shirakaba.db.statement.count` / `.duration` totals. Packages can
report their own events with `RequestScope::record()`.

---

<!-- guide/09-testing.md -->

# Testing

`TestClient` calls the application in-process, without a server:

```php
$client = new TestClient(TaskApi::builder(TaskSchema::database($file))->build());

$response = $client->post('/tasks', '{"title":"Write"}', ['Content-Type' => 'application/json']);
self::assertSame(201, $response->getStatusCode());
self::assertSame('Write', ResponseJson::at($response, '/title'));

$client->form('POST', '/tasks/1/attachments', ['note' => 'spec'], ['file' => $uploadedFile]);
```

- `ResponseJson::at($response, '/items/0/title')` reads JSON with a JSON Pointer.
- Building with `build()` in tests checks every route and handler, which also protects
  production code that uses `build(lazy: true)`.
- Use a real database in tests, for example a temporary SQLite file; per-request
  connections cannot share an in-memory SQLite database.
- To catch drift between documentation and behaviour, validate response bodies against the
  generated OpenAPI schemas, as `examples/tasks/tests/TaskApiTest.php` does.
- To catch N+1 queries, add a `StatementLog` observer and bound the statements a request
  runs: `self::assertLessThanOrEqual(3, count($log->last()), $log->describe())`.
  `$log->repeated()` lists statements that ran more than once.

---

<!-- guide/10-openapi.md -->

# OpenAPI

```sh
composer require --dev shirakaba/openapi
```

Documents are generated ahead of time from the same declarations that run the
application ([routing and handlers](../design/04-routing-and-handlers.md) and [JSON and OpenAPI](../design/06-json-and-openapi.md)):

```sh
vendor/bin/shirakaba-openapi app.php --config=openapi.php --output=openapi.json --strict
```

```php
<?php // openapi.php

return new Generator(
    new Info('Tasks', '1.0.0'),
    ['tasks.show' => new Operation(summary: 'Show a task', tags: ['tasks'])], // by route name
);
```

- Parameters, constraints and request bodies come from extractors and DTOs. A nullable
  path, query or header parameter is documented without null, since a request cannot
  carry one: with a `null` default it is optional, without one it is required.
- Doc comments on DTO properties (on the promoted constructor parameter, or the property
  of the same name) become property descriptions; tags such as `@var` are left out.
- Responses come from `#[JsonResponse]` and `#[Responds]` declarations, plus the Problem
  Details responses the core produces (400, 413, 415, 422, 401 and `default`).
- `#[Responds(200, contentType: 'application/activity+json')]` documents a body of another
  media type: any JSON value for JSON types, a string otherwise.
- `->undocumented()` on a route leaves it out, for endpoints of other protocols (WebFinger,
  ActivityPub) or internal ones.
- `#[Authenticated]` becomes a bearer security requirement.
- Anything that cannot be described is a warning and left out; `--strict` fails on
  warnings.

Commit the document and have a test regenerate and compare it, so it never drifts.
`ServeDocument` serves a pre-generated file if you want it online.

---

<!-- guide/11-deployment.md -->

# Deployment

## PHP-FPM

`shirakaba/runtime-fpm`, as in [Getting started](01-getting-started.md). Every request builds
the application; use `build(lazy: true)` so only the requested route is planned.

## FrankenPHP worker mode

```sh
composer require shirakaba/runtime-frankenphp
```

```php
<?php // public/index.php
new FrankenPhpRuntime()->run($builder->build());
```

```sh
frankenphp php-server --worker public/index.php
```

The application is built once and serves many requests (here eager `build()` is right).
After each request, unmoved uploads are removed and garbage is collected; after
`maxRequests` the worker restarts. The runtime conformance suite runs the same checks on
PHP-FPM, FrankenPHP, RoadRunner and Swoole, including that no state leaks between requests.

In worker mode, let the database keep its connection between requests instead of connecting
for each one ([database](../design/08-database.md)); it is rolled back and reset before the next request gets it:

```php
$database = new Database(static fn (): PDO => PDO::connect($dsn, $user, $password), reuse: true);
```

`php-server` sends every request to `public/index.php`. To serve the same entry point with
and without workers, choose the runtime there: under a worker, `$_SERVER['FRANKENPHP_WORKER']`
is set. Caddy compresses responses by default, which buffers Server-Sent Events; start
FrankenPHP with `--no-compress` (or exclude `text/event-stream` from encoding) when you stream.

## RoadRunner

```sh
composer require shirakaba/runtime-roadrunner
```

```php
<?php // worker.php
new RoadRunnerRuntime()->run($builder->build());
```

```yaml
# .rr.yaml
version: "3"
server:
  command: "php worker.php"
http:
  address: 0.0.0.0:8080
  pool:
    num_workers: 4
    max_jobs: 1000
```

```sh
rr serve
```

Each worker builds the application once and serves requests until RoadRunner stops it;
`max_jobs` restarts a worker after that many requests. RoadRunner stores uploads and removes
them after the request. It parses form bodies itself, so the body stream of a form request is
empty; read the fields with `#[FormBody]` or `getParsedBody()`. An exception that escapes the
application is logged by RoadRunner and answered with 500, and the worker keeps serving.

## Swoole

```sh
composer require shirakaba/runtime-swoole
```

```php
<?php // server.php
$server = new Swoole\Http\Server('0.0.0.0', 8080);
$server->set(['worker_num' => 4, 'max_request' => 1000, 'hook_flags' => SWOOLE_HOOK_ALL]);
new SwooleRuntime($server)->run($builder->build());
```

```sh
php server.php
```

The Swoole extension 6.2.5 or later is required. The application is built before the server
starts and copied into each worker; Shirakaba's database pools connect on first use, so
nothing is shared between workers. With `hook_flags`, blocking calls (database, sleeps,
sockets) yield to other requests, so one worker serves many requests at once, and a client
that disconnects from a stream is noticed while the handler waits. Requests get the `https`
scheme when the server's main port uses TLS. An exception that escapes the application goes
to the runtime's `$onError` callback (by default `error_log()`) and is answered with 500.

## Read-only root filesystems

Shirakaba writes nothing to disk at run time, so containers can run with a read-only root
filesystem (for example `ReadonlyRootFilesystem` on AWS ECS) once these have a writable
place:

- `/tmp` (or `upload_tmp_dir` and `sys_get_temp_dir()`): PHP keeps uploaded files there until
  they are moved, and `php://temp` streams spill there beyond 2 MB. Mount a small volume.
  RoadRunner (`http.uploads.dir`) and Swoole (`upload_tmp_dir`) keep their uploads there too.
- FrankenPHP: Caddy keeps data and configuration in `XDG_DATA_HOME` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`; mount
  volumes there or point them under `/tmp`. Terminating TLS at the load balancer and turning
  off automatic HTTPS leaves almost nothing to write.
- Sessions: use `DatabaseSessionStore`, which several instances also share, instead of
  `FileSessionStore`.

Logs go to standard error by default (`StreamLogger`), which container platforms collect.

## Behind a proxy

```php
$app->middleware(new TrustedProxies(['10.0.0.0/8'], [ForwardedHeader::For, ForwardedHeader::Proto]));
```

Forwarding headers are ignored unless the direct peer is a trusted proxy ([runtimes and scopes](../design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md)). Name
only the headers your proxy sets or overwrites: a header it passes through still carries
what the client sent. nginx's usual `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For
$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` and `X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme` match the example; trust
`ForwardedHeader::Host` only if the proxy also sets `X-Forwarded-Host`, or clients can
choose the host in the absolute URLs you build. `ForwardedHeader::Forwarded` (RFC 7239)
cannot be combined with the `X-Forwarded-*` headers.

Put it first, so later middleware sees the client's scheme, host and address
(`ClientAddress::of($request)`).

## Hosts and absolute URLs

Clients choose the `Host` header. Reject hosts the application does not serve, after
`TrustedProxies`:

```php
$app->middleware(
    new TrustedProxies(['10.0.0.0/8'], [ForwardedHeader::For, ForwardedHeader::Proto]),
    new AllowedHosts(['app.example.com', '*.app.example.com']),
);
```

Build links that leave the request, such as password-reset and confirmation URLs in
e-mails or OAuth redirect URIs, from a configured origin instead of the request URI:

```php
$origin = new CanonicalOrigin('https://app.example.com');
$link = $origin->url('/password-reset', ['token' => $token]);
```

## CORS

```php
$app->middleware(new Cors(['https://app.example.com'], allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization']));
```

## Streaming

`shirakaba/streaming` provides `Streamed` (chunked downloads) and `Sse` (Server-Sent Events).
Resources registered with `RequestScope::defer()` are released when the stream ends, not
when the handler returns ([runtimes and scopes](../design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md)). Typed events and publish/subscribe are in
[Real-time events](15-real-time-events.md).

---

<!-- guide/12-static-analysis.md -->

# Static analysis

Shirakaba is written for PHPStan at level `max`, and applications benefit from the same.

```sh
composer require --dev phpstan/phpstan shirakaba/phpstan
```

```neon
includes:
    - vendor/shirakaba/phpstan/extension.neon

parameters:
    level: max
    paths: [src, app.php]
    shirakaba:
        longRunningPaths: ['#/src/#']
        clockPaths: ['#/src/#']
        reportQueriesInLoops: true
```

`shirakaba/phpstan` reports:

- static properties, `global` and static variables in `longRunningPaths`, which would
  leak between requests under worker runtimes;
- middleware, handlers, extractors and resolvers that write to their own properties after
  construction;
- GET and HEAD handlers that take a database `Writer`, or a class built from one;
- in `clockPaths`, reads of the wall clock (`time()`, `date()` without a timestamp,
  `new DateTimeImmutable()`) outside a PSR-20 clock. Take a `Psr\Clock\ClockInterface`
  instead: `Shirakaba\Time\SystemClock` in production (always UTC), `FrozenClock` in tests;
- ORM calls checked against entity mappings (with `shirakaba/orm` installed): unknown
  properties in `where()`, `orderBy()`, `after()` and `Entities::patch()`, values of the
  wrong type for a property, unknown relations in `with()` and `whereHas()`, and
  projections passed to `into()` that do not match the relations requested in the same
  chain. Names may be spread from a constant array, as in `with(...self::RELATIONS)`;
  when a name is only known at run time, the projection is not checked;
- with `reportQueriesInLoops`, database calls inside loops, the usual shape of an N+1
  query.

It also types query results: `Select::from('tasks')->columns('id', 'title')->fetchAll($db)`
is `list<array{id: mixed, title: mixed}>` when the query is built in one chain with literal
column names (and `column($expression, 'alias')`), so a misspelt key is reported. Values stay
`mixed`, since the database decides their types; read them with checks or with `fetchInto()`.

Because applications are assembled in plain PHP, PHPStan also checks wiring, option types
and handler signatures that configuration files would hide.

---

<!-- guide/13-command-line.md -->

# Command line

`shirakaba/console` turns typed callables into commands ([background work](../design/10-background-work.md)), the way the core turns
them into HTTP handlers:

```php
$cli = new ConsoleBuilder('app', 'Commands of my application.');
$cli->command('users:import', static function (
    Output $output,
    #[Argument('CSV file to read')] string $file,
    #[Option('Report what would change')] bool $dryRun,
    #[Option('Rows per transaction')] int $batch = 500,
) use ($database): int {
    // ...
    $output->line('Imported 42 users.');

    return 0;
}, 'Imports users from a CSV file.');

exit($cli->build()->run($argv));
```

- Arguments are positional in declaration order; a default makes one optional, and a
  variadic parameter (`string ...$files`) takes the rest.
- Options are the parameter in kebab-case: `--dry-run`, `--batch=1000` or `--batch 1000`.
  A `bool` option is a flag with a `--no-` form; an `array` option collects repeated values;
  `#[Option(short: 'b')]` adds `-b`.
- Values are parsed strictly like request parameters: `int`, `float`, `bool`, backed enums,
  `DateTimeImmutable` (RFC 3339 with offset) and `LocalDate`.
- Help comes from the same declarations: `app help`, `app help users:import`,
  `app users:import --help`.
- `build()` fails on a parameter that cannot come from the command line, before any command
  runs.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Success, or what the command returns |
| 1 | An uncaught exception: its class and message on standard error, the trace with `--verbose` |
| 2 | A usage error: unknown command or option, missing or invalid value, or a `UsageError` the command throws |
| 130 | Interrupted: the command stopped with `RequestCancelled` |

## Long-running commands

A command that takes a `Cancellation` sees it requested on SIGINT and SIGTERM (with
`ext-pcntl`), so it can stop between units of work instead of being killed in the middle:

```php
$cli->command('reindex', static function (Cancellation $cancellation) use ($index): int {
    foreach ($index->batches() as $batch) {
        if ($cancellation->isRequested()) {
            return 0;
        }
        $index->rebuild($batch);
    }

    return 0;
});
```

## Framework commands in your console

Migrations and the OpenAPI document can live in the same binary as your commands:

```php
MigrationCommands::register($cli, static fn (): Migrations => new Migrations($database, $migrations, $entities), prefix: 'db:');
OpenApiCommand::register($cli, static fn (): AppBuilder => App::builder($database), static fn (): Generator => $generator);
```

`MigrationCommands` and `EntityCommands` come with `shirakaba/database-bridge`.
`examples/tasks/bin/tasks` shows a complete console. `shirakaba-migrate` and `shirakaba-openapi`
are built the same way.

## Inspecting the application

`RouteCommands` and `EntityCommands` answer what the code declares, for people and coding
agents alike:

```php
RouteCommands::register($cli, static fn (): AppBuilder => App::builder($database));
EntityCommands::register($cli, static fn (): array => [Task::class, Project::class], static fn () => $database->connect()->reader());
```

| Command | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `routes` | method, path, name and handler of every route |
| `routes:show tasks.update` or `routes:show "PATCH /tasks/{id}"` | the handler, each parameter (source, type, required, default, constraints) and the declared responses |
| `entities` | entity classes and their tables |
| `entities:show Task` (class, short name or table) | columns, relations, scopes and soft delete |
| `entities:check` | differences between the mappings and the database (exit 1 when there are any) |

`--json` prints a stable shape instead of text:

- `routes`: a list of `{method, path, name, handler, documented}`.
- `routes:show`: those fields plus `parameters` (`{source, name, parameter, type, required,
  default?, constraints?, mediaTypes?}`), `undescribedParameters`, `responses`
  (`{status, contentType, type, description}`) and `returns` (declared return classes).
- `entities`: a list of `{class, table}`.
- `entities:show`: `{class, table, columns, relations, defaultScopes, requiredScopes,
  softDelete}`; a column is `{property, column, type, kind, nullable, id, generated, managed,
  default?}` and a relation `{name, kind, entity, foreignKey, through?, localKey?, orderBy?}`.
- A `type` is `{kind, nullable, ...}`: `kind` is `string`, `int`, `float` or `bool` (with
  `format`), `enum` (`class`, `values`), `list` (`items`), `map` (`values`), `object` (`class`,
  `name`, `properties`, `additionalProperties`), `union` (`class`, `name`, `discriminator`,
  `members`), `const` (`value`), `file` (`mediaTypes`), `events` (`events`) or `mixed`.

## Testing

```php
$result = new ConsoleTester($cli->build())->run('users:import', 'users.csv', '--dry-run');
self::assertSame(0, $result->exitCode);
self::assertStringContainsString('Imported', $result->output);
```

---

<!-- guide/14-background-jobs.md -->

# Background jobs

`shirakaba/queue` runs work outside the request ([background work](../design/10-background-work.md)): sending mail, calling slow APIs,
recomputing data.

## Jobs and handlers

A job is a `#[JsonDto]` class; it is stored as JSON, never `serialize()`d. Handlers are
registered with a stable name, so renaming the class does not orphan waiting jobs:

```php
#[JsonDto]
final readonly class SendWelcome
{
    public function __construct(public int $userId) {}
}

$jobs = new Jobs(new DatabaseQueue($database));
$jobs->handle(SendWelcome::class, $mailer->sendWelcome(...), name: 'mail.welcome');
```

## Pushing in the transaction

```php
$writer->transaction(function (Writer $db) use ($jobs, $user): void {
    $user = Entities::insert($user, $db);
    $jobs->push(new SendWelcome($user->id), $db);
});
```

The database queue inserts the job in the same transaction, so a rolled-back sign-up never
sends mail and a committed one never loses its job. `PushOptions` sets the queue name, a
delay, a unique key (a second push while one is waiting does nothing) and the number of
attempts.

Add the table to your migrations: `'2026_11_12_create_jobs' => new CreateJobsTable()`.

## Delivery and retries

Delivery is at least once. A worker holds a job with a lease; if it crashes, the lease
expires and another worker runs the job again. Write handlers so that running twice is
harmless, for example by recording a unique key of the work done:

```php
public function sendWelcome(SendWelcome $job): void
{
    if (!Insert::into('sent_mails')->values(['key' => 'welcome-' . $job->userId])->onConflict(['key'])->execute($this->db)) {
        return; // already sent
    }
    // send
}
```

A handler that throws is retried with exponential backoff and jitter (`RetryPolicy`); after
the last attempt the job is kept as failed with the exception's class and message. Jobs of
unknown types and undecodable payloads are failed, never run.

## Handlers and request-scoped services

A handler receives the job and the `RequestScope` it runs in. Each job gets a fresh scope,
like a request, so request-scoped services are leased per job and released after it:

```php
$jobs->handle(SendWelcome::class, static function (SendWelcome $job, RequestScope $scope) use ($database, $mailer): void {
    $user = Entities::get(User::class, $job->userId, RequestDatabase::reader($database, $scope));
    $mailer->send($user->email, 'Welcome');
}, name: 'mail.welcome');
```

## Running workers

```php
$runner = new JobRunner($jobs, observers: [$logging, $tracing]);
QueueCommands::register($cli, static fn (): JobRunner => $runner, static fn (): DatabaseQueue => $queue);
```

```sh
app queue:work --queue=mail --queue=default --max-jobs=1000 --max-memory=256
app queue:failed
app queue:retry 42
app queue:forget 42
```

`queue:work` runs one job at a time. SIGTERM or SIGINT stops it after the current job, so a
deployment never kills a job halfway; `--max-jobs` and `--max-memory` make it exit so the
process manager starts a fresh one, as worker runtimes do after a number of requests. Run
it under systemd, Supervisor or as a container with a restart policy, and scale by running
more workers.

An idle worker on PostgreSQL does not poll: `DatabaseQueue` sends a NOTIFY when a job is
pushed (at commit), and the worker waits for it, so jobs start at once without `--sleep`
costing queries. `--rate=mail=5` keeps a worker to five jobs per second from the `mail` queue,
for providers with rate limits; each worker keeps its own limit, so divide by the number of
workers.

Observers see each job like a request: method `JOB`, the job's type as route, status 200
(succeeded), 503 (will be retried) or 500 (failed). The access log gets a line per job,
and the job's span is a child of the request that pushed it.

## A Redis queue

`shirakaba/queue-redis` keeps jobs in Redis instead of a table, for applications that keep the
queue's traffic off the database ([background work](../design/10-background-work.md)):

```php
$queue = new RedisQueue(RedisClient::fromUrl((string) getenv('REDIS_URL')), $clock);
$jobs = new Jobs($queue);
```

Each change is one Lua script, so workers never take the same job, and reservations carry a
lease and a token as with `DatabaseQueue`. The difference is pushing: the job reaches Redis
after the caller's transaction commits, so a rolled-back transaction pushes nothing, but a
process that dies between the commit and the push loses the job, and `push()` cannot tell yet
whether a job with the same unique key is waiting (it returns `true`; the duplicate is
dropped in Redis). Keep `DatabaseQueue` for jobs that must never be lost.

A handler that knows a job can never succeed throws `JobFailed`, which fails the job at once
instead of retrying it.

## Scheduled tasks

Recurring work is a schedule of jobs ([background work](../design/10-background-work.md)). Define it in PHP, add the runs table to
your migrations, and let system cron call one command every minute on every server:

```php
$schedule = new Schedule($jobs, new DateTimeZone('Asia/Tokyo'))
    ->job('sessions.gc', '*/15 * * * *', static fn (): object => new CollectSessions())
    ->job('reports.daily', '0 6 * * *', static fn (DateTimeImmutable $slot): object => new DailyReport($slot));

ScheduleCommands::register($cli, static fn (): Schedule => $schedule, static fn (): Writer => $database->connect()->writer());
// migrations: '2026_11_12_create_schedule_runs' => new CreateScheduleTable(),
// crontab:    * * * * * php bin/app schedule:run
```

Expressions have five fields (minute, hour, day, month, weekday 0-7) with `*`, ranges, lists
and steps, or `@hourly`, `@daily`, `@weekly`, `@monthly`, `@yearly`, read in the schedule's
time zone. Each task is queued once per minute however many servers run `schedule:run`; a
minute that passed while nothing ran is skipped. `schedule:list` shows the next and last runs.
In tests, call `$schedule->run($writer, $frozenClock)` and advance the clock.

## Testing

`JobRunner::runPending()` runs due jobs synchronously. `InMemoryQueue` accepts jobs when
the pushing transaction commits and lists them with `pendingTypes()`.

---

<!-- guide/15-real-time-events.md -->

# Real-time events

A browser keeps a Server-Sent Events stream open, and the server pushes an event whenever
something changes. `shirakaba/streaming` writes the stream and declares its events for OpenAPI;
`shirakaba/pubsub` carries changes from the requests that write them to the streams that wait
for them.

## Declaring and sending events

```php
#[SseResponse([
    'note' => NoteView::class,
    'noteDeleted' => NoteDeleted::class,
    'notification' => Notification::class,   // a #[JsonUnion]
])]
public function stream(RequestScope $scope, #[Db] Reader $db): Sse
{
    $subscription = $this->subscriber->subscribe($scope, ['notes', 'notifications']);

    return new Sse((function () use ($subscription, $db) {
        foreach ($subscription->messages(heartbeat: 15.0) as $message) {
            if ($message === null) {
                yield null;   // a keep-alive comment
                continue;
            }
            $view = $this->notes->visibleView((int) $message->payload, $db);
            if ($view !== null) {
                yield SseEvent::json($view, 'note', $message->payload);
            }
        }
    })());
}
```

`SseEvent::json()` writes the data with `Json`'s rules. OpenAPI describes the stream as a
string with an `x-itemSchema` listing each event and the type of its data, the shape
OpenAPI 3.2 uses for `itemSchema` ([real-time events](../design/11-real-time-events.md)), and the data types become components.

## Publishing changes

Publish with the writer that stores the change; subscribers receive the message when the
transaction commits, and never if it rolls back ([real-time events](../design/11-real-time-events.md)):

```php
$db->transaction(function (Writer $db) use ($note): void {
    $stored = Entities::insert($note, $db);
    $this->publisher->publish($db, 'notes', (string) $stored->id);
});
```

Send IDs, not data: each stream reads what its viewer may see, and PostgreSQL limits payloads
to under 8000 bytes. Channel names are letters, digits and underscores.

Wire `PostgresPubSub` (LISTEN/NOTIFY; open connections with `PDO::connect()`) as both
`Publisher` and `Subscriber`, and `InMemoryPubSub` in tests. A subscription ends with the
request scope, which for an `Sse` response is when the stream ends; `UNLISTEN` runs then.
`messages(heartbeat: 15.0, until: $openedAt->modify("+5 minutes"))` ends a stream at a
deadline without waiting for the next heartbeat.

## Capacity

Under PHP-FPM, the built-in server, FrankenPHP worker mode and RoadRunner alike, an open stream
holds a worker and a database connection until the client goes away, which is noticed only
when a write fails: four workers with four open streams answer nothing else. Swoole with
coroutine hooks serves other requests from the same worker while a stream waits, but each
stream still holds its database connection. Keep the heartbeat
short so closed streams are noticed, and size workers and connections for the number of open
streams.

For many streams, let a Mercure hub hold the connections ([real-time events](../design/11-real-time-events.md)). FrankenPHP has a
Mercure 1.0 hub built in; configure it in a Caddyfile, since its tokens name a trusted issuer:

```caddyfile
example.com {
	mercure {
		issuer https://example.com {
			publisher {
				jwt {env.MERCURE_KEY}
			}
			subscriber {
				jwt {env.MERCURE_KEY}
			}
		}
		resource_identifier https://example.com/.well-known/mercure
		anonymous    # public updates without a token
	}
	php_server
}
```

Issue tokens with `MercureTokens` and publish with `MercurePublisher` instead of
`PostgresPubSub`; it sends after commit like any `Publisher`:

```php
$tokens = new MercureTokens('https://example.com', 'https://example.com/.well-known/mercure', $key);
$publisher = new MercurePublisher($client, $factory, $factory, 'http://localhost/.well-known/mercure', $tokens, 'https://example.com/streams/', logger: $logger);

$publisher->publish($db, 'notes', (string) $note->id);                                   // public
$publisher->publishTo($db, $followerChannels, $json, private: true, event: 'note');      // one update, many topics
```

Browsers subscribe with `match` (Mercure 1.0 has no `topic` parameter):

```js
const events = new EventSource('/.well-known/mercure?match=' + encodeURIComponent('https://example.com/streams/users/42'));
```

Private updates reach only subscribers whose token grants the topic. Hubs read subscriber
tokens from the `Authorization` header or a cookie, never the URL, and `EventSource` cannot set
headers, so send the token as the cookie from a same-site response:

```php
$token = $tokens->subscriber('user-' . $user->id, ['https://example.com/streams/users/' . $user->id]);
return $response->withAddedHeader('Set-Cookie', $tokens->cookie($token));
```
