- Stores: `DatabaseSessionStore` (`shirakaba/session-database`) keys rows by the SHA-256 hash of the
  session ID, so reading the table does not hand out live sessions, and saves outside transactions so
  a request that rolls back keeps its session. `RedisSessionStore` (`shirakaba/session-redis`) answers
  503 when Redis cannot be reached rather than starting an empty session. `FileSessionStore` writes
  files readable only by their owner. Session data is JSON, never `serialize()`.

## Calling other servers

Applications call other servers: object storage, webhooks, and federated protocols whose URLs come
from other servers' documents. A URL chosen by someone else can point at loopback, the private network
or a cloud metadata endpoint (SSRF), answer slowly, send an endless body or redirect somewhere worse.
The checks must use the address actually connected to: checking a name and letting the transport
resolve it again allows DNS rebinding.

`shirakaba/http-client` provides `HttpClient`, a PSR-18 client on ext-curl, so signing libraries and
SDKs remain usable.

- The client resolves every host itself and checks every address; one refused address refuses the
  host. curl is then pinned to a checked address (`CURLOPT_RESOLVE`). By default only globally
  routable addresses are allowed (RFC 6890, with IPv4-mapped, NAT64 and compatible IPv6 judged by the
  embedded IPv4); `allowAddress` replaces the policy. Only http and https are allowed, and proxies
  from the environment are ignored.
- Redirects are followed by the client, not curl, up to `maxRedirects`, each hop resolved and checked
  again. 303, and 301/302 after POST, become GET without a body. `Authorization`, `Cookie` and
  `Proxy-Authorization` are dropped when the origin changes.
- `prepare` runs on every request sent, each redirect included, so signatures (HTTP Message
  Signatures, RFC 9421) cover the request actually sent.
- One `timeout` covers the whole exchange, redirects included; `connectTimeout` limits each
  connection; `maxResponseBytes` aborts the transfer as soon as more arrives. Responses are buffered in
  memory up to that limit.
- `$client->in($scope)` binds the client to a request: it stops when the request is cancelled or its
  deadline passes, and reports an event for every request sent, without path, query or headers.
- Failures are PSR-18 exceptions: `RequestRefused` (nothing was sent to the refused target) and
  `NetworkError` (with `timedOut` and `tooLarge`).

Tests that call a local server allow its address explicitly with `allowAddress`.

## Rate limits

Public endpoints need limits: sign-in attempts per address and per account, sign-ups per address,
posts per user, deliveries per remote server. A limit must hold across processes and servers, be
testable with a frozen clock, answer with a standard 429 and appear in the API description.

- `shirakaba/rate-limit`'s `RateLimiter` applies fixed windows: at most `limit` hits per `seconds` for
  each name and key. Fixed windows need one counter per window and one atomic upsert per hit; the
  price is that a client can make up to twice the limit across a window boundary, which is acceptable
  for abuse protection. Smoother algorithms can be added behind the same API.
- Limits are declared per route as middleware, `$limiter->limit($name, $limit, $seconds, $key)`,
  keyed by `RateKey::address()` (the client address from `shirakaba/trusted-proxy`, else
  `REMOTE_ADDR`), `RateKey::subject($id)` (the authenticated principal; anonymous requests are not
  counted) or `RateKey::custom()`. Handlers decide others with `hit()` or `attempt()`.
- Exceeding a limit throws `TooManyRequests`: a 429 with `Retry-After`, the IETF `RateLimit` and
  `RateLimit-Policy` headers and the problem code `rate-limited`. Route limits add the RateLimit
  headers to successful responses too, and declare the 429 so OpenAPI lists it.
- `DatabaseRateLimitStore` counts in one table shared by every process, with one upsert per hit on the
  request's connection. It refuses to count inside a transaction, whose rollback would undo the hit (a
  failed sign-in must still count). `prune()` deletes expired windows from a scheduled job. Keys are
  stored as SHA-256 digests, so addresses and user names are not kept in the table.
  `InMemoryRateLimitStore` serves tests.

---

<!-- design/10-background-work.md -->

# Commands, background jobs and scheduled tasks

## Command-line applications

Tools, queue workers and applications' own commands (imports, maintenance) share one small console
package, `shirakaba/console`, independent of the HTTP pipeline.

- Commands are typed callables, like handlers. Arguments and options are read from parameters with
  attributes:

  ```php
  $cli = new ConsoleBuilder('app');
  $cli->command('users:import', static function (
      #[Argument] string $file,
      #[Option] bool $dryRun = false,
      #[Option] int $batch = 500,
      Output $output,
  ): int { ... })->describe('Imports users from a CSV file.');
  $cli->build()->run($argv);
  ```

- Types are parsed strictly with the rules of request parameters (`int`, `bool`, backed enums,
  `DateTimeImmutable`, `LocalDate`); a bad value is a usage error naming the argument. Help text and
  usage come from the same metadata.
- Commands are planned when the console is built, so an unmappable parameter fails at `build()`, not
  when the command first runs.
- Exit codes are part of the contract: 0 success, 1 failure reported by the command, 2 usage error,
  130 interrupted. Uncaught exceptions print their class and message (a trace only with `--verbose`)
  and exit with 1.
- A command can ask for a `Cancellation` that is requested on SIGINT or SIGTERM (with `ext-pcntl`),
  so workers stop between jobs instead of being killed in the middle of one.
- Output goes through a small `Output` object; there is no formatting framework. Tests capture it
  with a test runner.
- Packages register their commands into the application's console (`MigrationCommands::register()`,
  `OpenApiCommand::register()`), and single-command tools declare a default command.

A general-purpose console library was not used: it is large, configured through classes and
inheritance, and duplicates what parameter types and attributes already say.

## Background jobs

Work that should not delay a response (sending mail, calling slow APIs, recomputing data) runs outside
the request. The usual failures are a job enqueued for a transaction that rolls back, a job lost
because the broker accepted it before the transaction committed, and a job run twice after a worker
crash. `shirakaba/queue` is designed around them.

- A `Queue` interface (push, reserve, acknowledge, release, fail) with a database driver
  (`DatabaseQueue`) and a Redis driver (`shirakaba/queue-redis`).
- **Jobs are data, handlers are code.** A job is a `#[JsonDto]` readonly class stored as JSON under a
  stable type name, never `serialize()`d. A handler is a callable registered for the job class with
  explicitly wired dependencies:

  ```php
  $jobs = new Jobs($queue);
  $jobs->handle(SendWelcomeMail::class, $mailer->sendWelcome(...), name: 'mail.welcome');
  $jobs->push(new SendWelcomeMail($user->id), $writer);
  ```

  A job of an unknown type is failed, never run.
- **Enqueueing joins the transaction.** With the database driver the job row is inserted in the
  caller's transaction, so it exists exactly when the business data does (a transactional outbox).
  The Redis driver pushes after commit with `afterCommit()`; a job can then be lost if the process
  dies between commit and push, which is the price of keeping the queue's writes off the database.
- **At-least-once delivery.** A worker reserves a job with a lease, using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on
  MySQL and PostgreSQL and a conditional update on SQLite (one Lua script per operation on Redis). A
  job whose lease expires is delivered again, so handlers must be idempotent; the guide shows how with
  a unique key. Exactly-once delivery is not achievable across a crash without idempotent handlers.
- **Retries** are counted per job with a bounded number of attempts and backoff with jitter from the
  PSR-20 clock. After the last attempt, or when a handler throws `JobFailed` for a permanent failure,
  the job is marked failed and kept for inspection and manual retry.
- **Delays and uniqueness.** Jobs can become available at a given instant; an optional unique key
  prevents duplicate pending jobs.
- **Workers are console commands.** `queue:work` reserves and runs jobs one at a time, stops between
  jobs on SIGTERM, and restarts itself after a number of jobs or an amount of memory. Each job runs in
  its own scope, like a request, with its own connection lease and cleanup, so nothing leaks between
  jobs. On PostgreSQL, idle workers can be woken with NOTIFY instead of polling.
- **Observability.** Jobs are reported to the same observers as requests (reserved, succeeded,
  retried, failed, with durations), and traces continue from the request that enqueued the job.
- **Testing.** An in-memory queue and a helper that runs pending jobs synchronously.

Running work after the response is sent (`fastcgi_finish_request()`, after-response hooks) was not
chosen: it has no retries, is lost on a crash and ties the work to the web process. A broker as the
only driver was not chosen either: it needs infrastructure many applications do not have and loses
the transactional outbox. Batches (run when every job of a group finished) and chains (run in order)
are not implemented yet.

## Scheduled tasks

Recurring work (session cleanup, pruning, reports) needs a schedule. System cron can call commands
directly, but then the schedule lives outside the application, is written per server and runs once
per server.

- The schedule is PHP code: `Schedule::job($name, $cron, $makeJob)` with five-field cron expressions
  (plus `@daily` and the like) evaluated in the schedule's time zone with the PSR-20 clock.
- System cron runs one command, `schedule:run`, every minute on every server. It pushes the job of each
  task due in the current minute and does not run the work itself, so the work gets the queue's
  retries, leases and observation.
- Each task runs once per minute slot however many servers call it: a row `(task, slot)` in
  `shirakaba_schedule_runs` is inserted in the same transaction as the job is pushed. A second server's
  insert fails on the key and it skips the task; a failed push rolls the claim back.
- Missed slots are not caught up. Work that must not be skipped checks what it has done itself (for
  example "report every day not yet reported"). Overlapping runs are prevented with the job's unique
  key.

## Redis

Sessions and the queue can use Redis or a compatible server (Valkey, ElastiCache). The `redis`
extension is not available everywhere, and a client library would be a third-party dependency, so
`shirakaba/redis` is a small client of its own:

- RESP2 over `stream_socket_client`, `redis://` and `rediss://` URLs (TLS with verified certificates),
  `AUTH` with a password or a user and password, `SELECT` of a database, timeouts on connecting and on
  every reply, and bounds on reply sizes;
- `command(...$arguments)` sends one command; `eval()` runs a Lua script, which is how the queue and
  the session store make their changes atomic;
- only stateless commands are offered (no `MULTI`, `WATCH`, `SUBSCRIBE`, or `SELECT` after
  connecting), so nothing a command leaves behind reaches the next request in a worker runtime. After
  an error that may have left a reply unread, the connection is closed and the next command
  reconnects.

It covers the commands Shirakaba uses, not pub/sub, clusters or RESP3.

---

<!-- design/11-real-time-events.md -->

# Real-time events

Real-time features need a change written by one request to reach clients waiting for it.
Shirakaba offers Server-Sent Events served by PHP for small numbers of streams, development and
tests, and a Mercure hub for many streams. Both publish after the writing transaction commits.

## Typed Server-Sent Events

`Sse` responses (`shirakaba/streaming`) stream events from a generator, with the request scope kept
open until the stream ends ([runtimes and scopes](03-runtimes-and-scopes.md)).

- `#[SseResponse(['note' => NoteView::class, 'ping' => 'string'])]` on a handler declares its events,
  like `#[JsonResponse]`. Data types are `#[JsonDto]` or `#[JsonUnion]` classes, or `string`.
  `SseEvent::json($dto, 'note')` writes data with `Json`'s rules.
- Descriptions gain an `EventStreamType` (event name to data type).
- OpenAPI 3.1 cannot type the items of a stream. The document keeps `schema: {type: string}` for the
  stream and adds `x-itemSchema`, written exactly as OpenAPI 3.2's `itemSchema` for
  `text/event-stream`: an object with `event`, `data`, `id` and `retry`, `event` and `data` required,
  and a `oneOf` with one variant per event whose `event` is a `const` and whose `data` is a string with
  `contentMediaType: application/json` and `contentSchema` referencing the data type. When Shirakaba
  writes OpenAPI 3.2, the key becomes `itemSchema` and nothing else changes.
- The declaration is not checked against what the handler yields.

## Publish/subscribe

`shirakaba/pubsub` connects writers and streams with two interfaces.

- `Publisher::publish(Writer $db, $channel, $payload)` takes the writer, so delivery follows its
  transaction: subscribers receive the message after commit, never after a rollback.
- `Subscriber::subscribe(RequestScope $scope, $channels)` returns a `Subscription` that ends when the
  scope closes; for an `Sse` response, that is when the stream ends. `next($timeout)` waits for one
  message; `messages($heartbeat)` yields messages and a `null` after each silent interval, which `Sse`
  sends as a keep-alive, and stops when the request is cancelled.
- `PostgresPubSub` implements both on LISTEN/NOTIFY: `pg_notify()` on the writer (PostgreSQL delivers
  at commit by itself), `LISTEN` on the request's connection and `UNLISTEN *` when the scope closes.
  Both run through the connection, so they appear in the statement log. Payloads are small (under 8000
  bytes): send IDs and let the subscriber read the data with its own permissions.
- `InMemoryPubSub` implements both in one process, delivering through `afterCommit()`, for tests.
- Channel names for these implementations are identifiers (letters, digits and underscores, at most 63
  characters), so they can be quoted safely. Other brokers implement the same interfaces in their own
  packages, publishing from `afterCommit()` to keep the commit guarantee.

## Many streams through a hub

An `Sse` response holds a PHP worker, and with `PostgresPubSub` a database connection, for as long as
the stream is open. A handful of open streams can exhaust a small worker pool, worker mode does not
change that, and a closed browser is noticed only at the next write. A runtime that multiplexes
connections would change the execution model of the whole application, and one LISTEN connection per
process would still hold a worker per stream. Instead, the application publishes to a hub that holds
the browser connections. Mercure is an open protocol, and FrankenPHP has a hub built in.

- `MercurePublisher` implements `Publisher` for Mercure. It posts updates to the hub after the writer's
  transaction commits, so the commit guarantee holds, and takes any PSR-18 client. Channels become
  topics through a prefix; updates can be private. There is no PHP-side Mercure subscriber: the point
  is that PHP does not hold the connection.
- It follows Mercure 1.0. `MercureTokens` issues publisher and subscriber tokens as RFC 9068 access
  tokens (`typ: at+jwt`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and grants in `authorization_details` entries with
  `actions` and `topics`), signed with HS256, with `iat` and `exp` from the PSR-20 clock and a random
  `jti`, and builds the subscriber cookie (`__Secure-mercure_access_token`, Secure, HttpOnly).
  Subscriber tokens therefore reach `EventSource` only as a same-site cookie; a hub on another site
  needs a fetch-based client that sends the `Authorization` header.
- `publishTo($db, $channels, $payload, private:, event:)` sends one update to several channels and
  chooses privacy and the SSE event per update.
- With a logger, hub failures after commit are logged and skipped; without one they are thrown.
  Callers that need retries publish through a queued job.
- The integration test runs against the hub built into FrankenPHP, configured with a Caddyfile.

## Typed hub events

Hub updates are a channel name and a string, described nowhere. Typed channels give them a contract
that clients can generate code from.

- A channel is a class declared with `#[EventChannel('board/{boardId}', private: true, summary:
  '...')]` and one `#[ChannelEvent('card.added', CardAdded::class)]` per event. Its constructor's
  promoted public parameters are exactly the template's variables (strings, integers or backed enums).
  Event classes are `#[JsonDto]`s that do not declare `type` themselves; event types are lower-case
  words joined by dots or underscores.
- The event kind is a `type` property inside the JSON payload, and updates are published without an
  SSE event name, so every update reaches `EventSource.onmessage`. Ordering data belongs in the
  payload.
- Topics are built from the template with each parameter percent-encoded, appended to the publisher's
  topic prefix; `MercureTokens` builds subscribe claims from channel instances the same way, so a token
  and the topic it must match cannot disagree. Mercure channel names are path segments of unreserved
  characters and percent-encodings, up to 1024 characters.
- `MercureEvents::publish($db, $channels, $event)` writes `{"type": ..., ...fields}`, publishes after
  commit, privately when the channel says so, and refuses an event the channel does not declare.
  Several instances of one channel class become one update with several topics.
- `EventChannels::describe(...)` turns channel classes into descriptions, and the OpenAPI generator
  writes them under a root `x-event-channels` extension:

  ```yaml
  x-event-channels:
    board:
      summary: Updates every participant of a board may see
      channel: 'board/{boardId}'
      parameters:
        boardId: {type: string}
      private: true
      content:
        application/json:
          schema: {$ref: '#/components/schemas/BoardEvent'}
  ```

  `BoardEvent` is a `oneOf` of the payload components with a `discriminator` on `type`, each member
  requiring `type` as a `const`.

The hub URL and the topic prefix stay deployment configuration, outside the document. A payload class
also used as an API response gets one component, so event payloads are best kept as their own classes.

---

<!-- design/12-mail-and-templates.md -->

# Mail and templates

Applications send mail: address confirmations, password resets, notifications. A mail needs a
subject, a plain-text body and usually an HTML body, often in the recipient's language, and must
leave only once the data it describes is committed. Mail has its own risks: header injection through
a subject or display name, HTML bodies built from user input, credentials sent without TLS, and slow
SMTP servers holding up a request. Non-ASCII subjects and names need RFC 2047 encoding, which
hand-written headers get wrong. The dependency policy rules out the usual mail and template
libraries, so Shirakaba has its own, kept small.

## Templates

`shirakaba/template` is a separate package, so plain-text exports or pages can use it too.

- Templates are files under one directory, loaded by name, never by a path from user input; `..` and
  absolute names are refused.
- The data is a readonly object, not an array. Templates read its public properties and those of
  nested objects (`{{ user.name }}`): no method calls, no function calls, no arithmetic. A template
  cannot run code, so it cannot leak data or call services; the price is that every formatted value is
  prepared in PHP.
- The syntax is small and fixed:
  - `{{ path }}` prints a value;
  - `{% if path %}`, `{% elseif path %}`, `{% else %}`, `{% endif %}`, with `not`; conditions test
    booleans, empty strings, empty lists and null, nothing else;
  - `{% for item in path %}` ... `{% else %}` ... `{% endfor %}` over lists;
  - `{% layout "name" %}` wraps the template in a layout that prints `{{ content }}`;
  - `{# comment #}`.

  A block tag or comment alone on its line removes the line, so text templates do not fill with blank
  lines. Filters, macros, includes and expressions are left out until an application needs them.
- Printable values are `string`, `int`, `Stringable` and `Html`. Anything else is an error, so
  formatting (dates, amounts, plurals) happens in typed PHP code.
- Escaping follows the file type: `.html` templates escape with `htmlspecialchars` (`ENT_QUOTES |
  ENT_SUBSTITUTE`, UTF-8); `.txt` templates print as is. An `Html` value (markup the application
  vouches for) is printed unescaped in HTML and refused in text. There is no `raw` filter.
- Templates are parsed into an immutable tree, kept per name in the application-scoped engine. Nothing
  is compiled to PHP or evaluated, so no writable directory is needed. Errors name the template, line
  and column.
- `TemplateChecker` (a test helper and the `templates:check` command) parses every template and, for
  templates declared with their data class, checks every path against that class's property types,
  including the item types of `list<T>`. Typos fail in CI instead of in a sent mail.
- Locales are a parameter, not global state: `render('welcome.txt', $data, 'ja-JP')` looks for
  `welcome.ja-JP.txt`, then `welcome.ja.txt`, then `welcome.txt`.

A template engine for HTML pages would start from this syntax and add attribute, URL and script
contexts.

## Mail

`shirakaba/mailer` needs ext-openssl for TLS and no third-party library.

- `Email` is an immutable value: `from`, `to`, `cc`, `bcc`, `replyTo`, `subject`, `text`, an optional
  `html`, attachments and extra headers. `Address` validates the address and refuses CR, LF and NUL in
  the address and the display name. Header names and values are checked the same way, so no header can
  be injected.
- `Mailer` has one method, `send(Email): SentEmail` (the Message-ID and the size).
- MIME is written by the package: `multipart/alternative` for text and HTML, `multipart/mixed` for
  attachments, `multipart/related` for inline images; quoted-printable bodies, RFC 2047 encoded words
  for non-ASCII headers, CRLF line endings and lines folded under 998 octets. `Date` comes from the
  PSR-20 clock and Message-ID from `random_bytes` and the sender's domain. Addresses with a non-ASCII
  local part are refused (SMTPUTF8 is not supported); non-ASCII domains are converted with IDNA when
  ext-intl is present.
- `SmtpTransport` speaks SMTP over `stream_socket_client`: implicit TLS (465) or STARTTLS (587),
  STARTTLS required by default, certificates verified, AUTH PLAIN and LOGIN only after TLS, timeouts
  on connecting and on every reply, a bound on reply length, and dot-stuffing.
  `SmtpTransport::fromDsn()` reads one `smtp://` or `smtps://` string for convenience.
- `TemplatedEmail` joins mail and templates: a mail template is `name.subject.txt`, `name.txt` and an
  optional `name.html`. The subject is rendered, trimmed and refused if it contains a line break.
- Every send can be reported as an `EmailSent` event (transport, recipient count, size, duration, error
  kind) without addresses, subject or content; `ObservedMailer($mailer, $scope)` does the reporting
  where a request or job scope exists.
- Testing: `RecordingMailer` keeps sent mail for assertions (the rendered text and HTML, links in the
  body); `NullMailer` and `LogMailer` (to a PSR-3 logger) do not send. The SMTP client is tested
  against a scripted connection, and against a local SMTP test server when `SHIRAKABA_TEST_SMTP_DSN` is
  set.

Providers' HTTP APIs, DKIM signing, bounce handling, Markdown bodies, HTML-to-text conversion, CSS
inlining and receiving mail are not part of the package.

## Sending outside the request

An SMTP exchange takes long and fails in ways a request should not wait for.

- `QueuedMailer` (`shirakaba/mailer-queue`, so the mailer itself needs no queue or database) is a
  `Mailer` built per request from the request's Writer. It pushes a `SendEmail` job in the caller's
  transaction, so the mail leaves only when the data is committed, with the queue's retries
  ([background work](10-background-work.md)). A permanent failure (SMTP 5xx) fails the job without
  retrying it. A retried job reuses its Message-ID so receivers can drop duplicates.
- Attachments travel in the job up to a size limit. For mail built from database rows, an application
  job (`SendWelcomeMail { userId }`) that renders when it runs is better, so the mail shows the data at
  sending time.
- A queued mail waits in the job's payload, and a failed job keeps it. Mail carrying a secret (a
  one-time code) is sent with `Writer::afterCommit()` instead, which is also faster for the waiting
  user.

---

<!-- design/13-static-analysis-and-agents.md -->

# Static analysis and coding agents

## PHPStan at level max

All code passes PHPStan at level `max` with strict rules and the extra strictness options in
`phpstan.dist.neon`. Baselines and `@phpstan-ignore` are not used: a type is fixed or narrowed with a
check. Configuration as code ([principles](01-principles.md)) exists largely so that PHPStan sees the
whole application.

`shirakaba/phpstan` adds rules for applications:

| Rule | Reports |
|---|---|
| `SafeMethodHandlerRule` | a GET or HEAD handler that takes a `Writer` or a class built from one |
| `NoSharedMutableStateRule` | mutable static properties and global variables in package code |
| `NoStateInAppScopedObjectRule` | request data kept in properties of middleware, handlers or extractors |
| `NoAmbientClockRule` | reads of the wall clock other than a PSR-20 clock |
| `EntityQueryRule` | unknown columns and relations, and value types that do not match the mapping |
| `RequiredScopeRule` | a query of a scoped entity that cannot have its required scope |
| `QueryInLoopRule` | queries inside loops, the usual source of N+1 queries |

`SelectResultTypeExtension` gives query results their row shapes.

## Effects and Steins

[Steins](https://github.com/rigortype/steins) is a PHP type checker modelled on PHPStan that adds an
effect system: it infers what a function can do to the outside world (`io.db`, `io.net.http`,
`nondet.time`, ...) and checks it against declared upper bounds called envelopes. It reads PHPStan's
purity tags, including `@phpstan-impure <label>`.

- Pure code is marked `@phpstan-pure`; code with known effects is marked `@phpstan-impure <label>`
  using Steins' label vocabulary (`io`, `io.db`, `io.output`, `global.read`, `nondet.time`,
  `nondet.random`). The tags are useful to PHPStan today and become effect envelopes under Steins.
- Only PHPDoc tags are used: no Steins attributes and no runtime change. Generic attribute scanners in
  applications that instantiate every attribute would fail when the attribute class is absent, and
  requiring it would force a pre-release dependency on users.
- `composer steins` runs a pinned Steins version over the packages with the strict profile. CI runs it
  as a non-blocking job. Envelopes on public extension points are added only where the bound is
  certain, since a wrong bound becomes a breaking change for implementers once it is enforced.

The guarantee is stated honestly. The goal is to prove that handlers for safe methods (GET, HEAD) do
not write to a database, but Steins cannot show it yet: `io.db` has no read and write sub-labels, PDO
is not in its catalogue, and handlers registered as closures are unknown callees. Until it can, the
`Reader`/`Writer` split checked by `SafeMethodHandlerRule` is the enforcement, which is weaker than an
effect proof. Observation, logging and cache writes are allowed effects even for safe methods; the
policy covers application writes only. "Statically verifiable" is never claimed beyond what is proven.

## Support for coding agents

Coding agents write much application code, and Shirakaba is not in any model's training data: an
agent left alone guesses its API from other frameworks and gets it wrong. Shirakaba already gives
agents a lot to check against (PHPStan rules, `describe()`, OpenAPI generation, schema checks,
migration lint and diff, test helpers); what they lack is knowledge of Shirakaba itself. The approach
follows the one Next.js documents for the same problem.

- **Version-matched documentation ships as one package, `shirakaba/docs`**, installed as
  `vendor/shirakaba/docs/`: the guide, these design documents, an API index, error pages and problem
  code pages. Its version always matches the framework's, because all packages are released together.
  One package was chosen over docs in each package because the guide crosses packages.
- **`AGENTS.md` is updated only by an explicit command**, `shirakaba-docs agents:sync`, never by
  Composer hooks or at runtime. It writes a block between markers, keeps everything else, and tells
  agents that Shirakaba is not in their training data and where to read. `--claude` also makes
  `CLAUDE.md` import `AGENTS.md` for agents that read only that file.
- **Commands instead of a server.** Shirakaba has no long-running development server, and what an agent
  needs to inspect can be printed: routes, entities, schema checks, migrations and OpenAPI are console
  commands with plain-text and JSON output. An MCP server would be reconsidered only for a need that
  commands cannot meet.
- **Errors carry codes and fixes.** Build-time errors and Problem Details have stable codes with a page
  each that lists the fixes and their trade-offs; messages end with the path of that page.
- **Online formats come from the same source.** `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` are generated from
  `shirakaba/docs` by `composer docs:generate`, and a test fails while they are stale.
- **Skills only for workflows** that span several steps (adding an endpoint, adding an entity with its
  migration, auditing N+1 queries, adding a background job); facts belong in the documentation.
- **Effects are measured.** `tools/evals/` holds agent tasks on a fresh application with checks that
  decide success, run with and without the bundled documentation.

Documentation is part of every change's definition of done: an API change updates `shirakaba/docs` in
the same commit.

---

<!-- messages/db-parameter.md -->

# db-parameter: #[Db] needs a Reader, a Writer or a class built from one

`#[Db]` gives a handler the request's database access ([database](../design/08-database.md)). It accepts `Reader`,
`Writer`, or a class whose constructor takes exactly one `Reader` or `Writer` plus, optionally,
services typed with classes or interfaces ([database](../design/08-database.md)). Anything else (`PDO`, `Database`,
`Connection`, a class with two database parameters) fails the build.

## Fixes

**A. Ask for the access you need.** `#[Db] Reader $db` for reads, `#[Db] Writer $db` for
writes. A GET or HEAD handler must not take a Writer; shirakaba/phpstan reports it.

**B. Wrap queries in a class.** A class with one Reader or Writer parameter keeps SQL out of
handlers and documents what the handler may do:

```php
final readonly class TaskQueries
{
    public function __construct(private Reader $db) {}

    public function find(TaskId $id): ?TaskView { /* ... */ }
}

public function show(#[Path] TaskId $id, #[Db] TaskQueries $tasks): Json
```

**C. Add services next to the Reader or Writer.** Other constructor parameters come from the
request scope by type; register them once with `new Provide([ClockInterface::class =>
$clock])`. Trade-off: a missing service fails the request, not the build.

## Common mistakes

- Taking `PDO` or `Database`: the connection belongs to the request and is released with it;
  never hold it yourself.
- Two database parameters in one class: split it into a query class and a command class.
- An untyped or scalar extra parameter (`string $bucket`): wrap configuration in a class and
  provide that.

---

<!-- messages/handler-parameter.md -->

# handler-parameter: a handler parameter has no source

Shirakaba never guesses where a handler argument comes from ([routing and handlers](../design/04-routing-and-handlers.md)). Every parameter needs an
extractor attribute that says so, or one of the two types the core injects: the PSR-7
`ServerRequestInterface` and the `RequestScope`. The application fails to build otherwise,
before any request is served.

## Fixes

**A. Say where the value comes from.** Use `#[Path]`, `#[Query]`, `#[Header]` or `#[Cookie]`
for single values, `#[JsonBody]` (shirakaba/json) or `#[FormBody]` (shirakaba/form) for the body,
`#[Authenticated]` (shirakaba/auth) for the user, and `#[Db]` (shirakaba/database) for database
access. This is almost always the fix.

**B. Take the service from the handler's own constructor.** Application services (a clock,
a mailer, an HTTP client) are not request data. Give them to the handler object when you wire
the application, or to a `#[Db]` class through the `Provide` middleware ([database](../design/08-database.md)). Trade-off:
the handler must be an object rather than a closure.

**C. Read the request yourself.** Declare `ServerRequestInterface $request` and read it.
Trade-off: the value is untyped, unvalidated and missing from OpenAPI; prefer A.

## Example

```php
final readonly class TaskHandlers
{
    public function __construct(private ClockInterface $clock) {}

    public function update(
        #[Path] TaskId $id,
        #[JsonBody] TaskPatch $input,
        #[Db] TaskCommands $tasks,
        #[Authenticated] User $user,
    ): Json {
        // ...
    }
}

$app->patch('/tasks/{id}', $handlers->update(...))->name('tasks.update');
```

## Common mistakes

- Expecting dependency injection by type, as in Laravel or Symfony: Shirakaba has no container
  ([principles](../design/01-principles.md)).
- Leaving out `#[Path]` because the name matches the `{id}` placeholder: the name is not
  enough.
- Declaring `Request` or a framework-specific request class: use `ServerRequestInterface`.

---

<!-- messages/mutable-date-time.md -->

# mutable-date-time: use DateTimeImmutable for instants

JSON DTOs, entities and extractors take instants as `DateTimeImmutable` and calendar dates as
`LocalDate` ([date and time](../design/07-date-and-time.md)). `DateTime` is mutable, so a value shared between objects can change
under them, and `DateTimeInterface` does not say which one arrives.

## Fixes

**A. Declare `DateTimeImmutable` for a point in time.** JSON reads it from an RFC 3339
string with an offset (`2026-11-11T09:30:00Z`) and writes it in UTC.

**B. Declare `LocalDate` for a calendar date.** Birthdays, due dates and other values without
a time of day: `2026-11-11` in JSON, a `DATE` column in the database.

## Example

```php
#[JsonDto]
final readonly class TaskView
{
    public function __construct(
        public int $id,
        public DateTimeImmutable $createdAt,
        public ?LocalDate $dueOn,
    ) {}
}
```

Take the current time from a PSR-20 clock (`ClockInterface::now()`), not `new
DateTimeImmutable()`, so tests can freeze it.

## Common mistakes

- Accepting date-times without an offset: Shirakaba rejects `2026-11-11T09:30:00` because it
  does not say which instant it is.
- Storing local wall-clock times: instants are stored and returned in UTC.

---

<!-- messages/projection-mismatch.md -->

# projection-mismatch: the projection does not match the requested relations

`into(Projection::class)` fills the projection's constructor ([database](../design/08-database.md)):

- a parameter typed with the entity class receives the entity;
- a parameter named like a requested relation receives it (a list for to-many relations);
- `<relation>Count` receives a `withCount()` count;
- any other parameter receives the entity property of the same name;
- `#[From('name')]` takes another name, and `#[Computed]` takes a value you pass in.

Every requested relation needs a parameter, and every parameter needs one of these sources.
The check runs before any query, and shirakaba/phpstan runs it too.

## Fixes

**A. Request the relation, or remove the parameter.** If the projection has `User $user`,
call `->with('user')`; if you did not mean to load it, drop the parameter.

**B. Add a parameter for each requested relation.** For nested paths, the parameter's class
is itself a projection: `#[Items(CommentView::class)] array $comments` for lists.

**C. Rename with `#[From]`.** `#[From('notifier')] UserView $user` receives the `notifier`
relation under another name.

**D. Mark values that do not come from the entity `#[Computed]`.** Pass them with the
`$computed` callback of `into()`, which receives all loaded entities (and, as a second list,
the related entities of nested projections with computed parameters) so one query serves the
page. Trade-off: the values are yours to compute and batch.

## Example

```php
final readonly class NoteView
{
    /** @param list<FileView> $files */
    public function __construct(
        public string $id,
        public string $text,
        public UserView $user,
        #[Items(FileView::class)] public array $files,
        #[Computed] public array $reactions = [],
    ) {}
}

$views = Entities::query(Note::class)
    ->with('user', 'files')
    ->into(NoteView::class, $db, static fn (array $notes): array => array_map(
        static fn (Note $note): array => ['reactions' => $counts[$note->id] ?? []],
        $notes,
    ));
```

## Common mistakes

- A parameter named after a column (`user_id`) rather than the property (`userId`).
- Requesting `comments.author` but declaring `array $comments` without `#[Items(...)]`: the
  nested relation needs a projection class to land in.

---

<!-- messages/scope-missing.md -->

# scope-missing: a query of a scoped entity has no scope

An entity with `#[RequiredScope(InTenant::class)]` can only be queried, updated or deleted
with that scope passed. Forgetting the tenant fails loudly instead of returning
or changing another tenant's rows. The check applies to `Entities::query()`, `get()`,
`find()`, writes by key, bulk updates and deletes, and relations loaded with `with()`.

## Fixes

**A. Pass the scope.** The value usually comes from the request (the signed-in user's
tenant):

```php
Entities::query(Task::class)->scoped(new InTenant($user->tenantId))->fetch($db);
Entities::get(Task::class, $id, $db, scopes: [new InTenant($user->tenantId)]);
```

**B. Switch it off on purpose.** Administrative code that must read across tenants names the
scope: `->withoutScope(InTenant::class)`. Trade-off: every such line is a place to review;
keep them few and obvious.

**C. Put the scope in a query class.** A `#[Db]` class built with the tenant (through
`Provide` or a constructor argument) applies it everywhere, so handlers cannot forget it.

## Common mistakes

- Making the scope a `#[DefaultScope]` to silence the error: default scopes take no request
  data and cannot express a tenant.
- Filtering with `->where('tenantId', ...)` instead of `->scoped(...)`: the check does not know
  about plain conditions, and related entities stay unfiltered.

---

<!-- messages/unknown-relation.md -->

# unknown-relation: the entity declares no such relation

`with()`, `withWhere()`, `withCount()`, `whereHas()`, `whereDoesntHave()` and `#[From]` name
relations, and relations exist only when the entity class declares them ([database](../design/08-database.md)). Relations
are never inferred from property names or foreign keys, and never loaded on access.

## Fixes

**A. Declare the relation on the entity.**

```php
#[Table('notes')]
#[BelongsTo('user', User::class, 'userId')]                                   // notes.user_id
#[HasMany('replies', Note::class, 'replyId', orderBy: 'id')]                  // notes.reply_id
#[ManyToMany('files', DriveFile::class, through: 'note_files', localKey: 'note_id', foreignKey: 'file_id', orderBy: 'position')]
final readonly class Note { /* ... */ }
```

**B. Fix the name.** Names are the first argument of the attribute, case-sensitive; dotted
paths name a relation at each step (`reply.user` needs `reply` on Note and `user` on the
reply's entity). Run `app entities:show Note` to list them.

**C. Read it with a separate query.** When the data is not really a relation (a computed
value, another system), query it yourself and pass it in with `#[Computed]`.
Trade-off: you batch it yourself.

## Common mistakes

- Expecting `$note->user` to load lazily: entities are plain readonly objects; ask for
  relations with `with()` and read them through a projection.
- Using the column or property name (`userId`) instead of the relation name (`user`).

---

<!-- problems/body-too-large.md -->

# body-too-large

**Status 413.** The body exceeds the endpoint's size limit, has too many object members or form
fields, or an uploaded file exceeds the upload limit.

- **Client:** send less, or split the request.
- **Server:** limits are options of `#[JsonBody]` (`maxBytes`, `maxMembers`) and `#[FormBody]`, and
  PHP's upload settings.

---

<!-- problems/constraint.md -->

# constraint

**Field error.** The value has the right type but breaks a constraint: a length, a range, a
pattern, an e-mail address, a file type, or the DTO's own check of the combination. The `detail`
says which.

- **Client:** correct the value as the `detail` describes; the OpenAPI document lists the limits
  (`minLength`, `maximum`, `pattern`, ...).

---

<!-- problems/invalid-body.md -->

# invalid-body

**Status 400.** A JSON or form body does not match the expected structure: missing or unknown
fields, wrong types, values that cannot be parsed. Each problem is listed in `errors` with a JSON
Pointer, a `detail` and a field code ([required](required.md), [unknown-field](unknown-field.md),
[invalid-type](invalid-type.md), [invalid-date-time](invalid-date-time.md),
[invalid-date](invalid-date.md), [invalid-choice](invalid-choice.md)).

- **Client:** fix each field listed in `errors`.
- **Server:** the structure is the DTO of `#[JsonBody]` or `#[FormBody]`.

---

<!-- problems/invalid-choice.md -->

# invalid-choice

**Field error.** The value is not one of the allowed values of an enum, or a union's
discriminator names no member. The `detail` lists the allowed values.

- **Client:** send one of the listed values; they are case-sensitive.

---

<!-- problems/invalid-date-time.md -->

# invalid-date-time

**Field error, or problem code of a parameter.** The value is not an RFC 3339 date-time with an
offset. Shirakaba requires the offset because `2026-11-11T09:30:00` does not say which instant it
is.

- **Client:** send `2026-11-11T09:30:00Z` (UTC) or `2026-11-11T18:30:00+09:00`. In JavaScript,
  `new Date().toISOString()` produces a valid value; a `datetime-local` input does not, so convert
  it first.
- **Server:** a value that is a calendar date without a time belongs in a `LocalDate`, which takes
  `YYYY-MM-DD` ([invalid-date](invalid-date.md)).

---

<!-- problems/invalid-date.md -->

# invalid-date

**Field error, or problem code of a parameter.** The value is not a calendar date in the form
`YYYY-MM-DD`, or it is not a real date (`2026-02-30`).

- **Client:** send `2026-11-11`, without a time or an offset.

---

<!-- problems/invalid-parameter.md -->

# invalid-parameter

**Status 400.** A path, query, header or cookie parameter has a value of the wrong type (`page=x`
for an integer, an unknown enum value) or breaks a constraint (`#[Range]`, `#[Length]`). The
`detail` names the parameter and what was expected; the received value is never echoed.

- **Client:** send a value of the documented type and range.
- **Server:** the expectation comes from the handler parameter's type and constraint attributes.

Dates and date-times get [invalid-date-time](invalid-date-time.md) or
[invalid-date](invalid-date.md) instead.

---

<!-- problems/invalid-type.md -->

# invalid-type

**Field error.** The value has the wrong JSON type (a string where a number is expected, an
array where an object is expected) or a structure the endpoint does not accept (a repeated form
field, a nested multipart part).

- **Client:** send the type the OpenAPI document declares. JSON numbers are not strings: send
  `5`, not `"5"`.

---

<!-- problems/invalid-values.md -->

# invalid-values

**Status 422.** The body has the right structure, but values break constraints (`#[Length]`,
`#[Range]`, `#[Email]`, ...) or the DTO rejected the combination. Each entry of `errors` has the
code [constraint](constraint.md).

- **Client:** correct the listed values.
- **Server:** constraints are attributes on the DTO's constructor parameters.

---

<!-- problems/malformed-body.md -->

# malformed-body

**Status 400.** The body is not valid JSON, or nests deeper than allowed.

- **Client:** send well-formed JSON (`JSON.stringify` in JavaScript), UTF-8 encoded.

---

<!-- problems/missing-parameter.md -->

# missing-parameter

**Status 400.** A required path, query, header or cookie parameter was not sent. The `detail`
names it, for example `Missing query parameter "page".`

- **Client:** send the parameter; the OpenAPI document marks required parameters.
- **Server:** give the handler parameter a default (`#[Query] int $page = 1`) or make it nullable
  to make it optional.

---

<!-- problems/rate-limited.md -->

# rate-limited

**Status 429.** The client made more requests of this kind than the limit allows in the current
window, such as sign-in attempts per address or posts per user. `Retry-After` says how many
seconds to wait; the `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers give the limit, what is left and
when the window resets.

- **Client:** wait for `Retry-After` seconds before trying again; do not retry in a loop.
- **Server:** limits are declared per route with `RateLimiter::limit()` or checked in a handler
  with `RateLimiter::hit()` (shirakaba/rate-limit).

---

<!-- problems/repeated-parameter.md -->

# repeated-parameter

**Status 400.** A parameter that takes one value appeared more than once, as in
`?page=1&page=2`. Shirakaba does not pick one silently.

- **Client:** send it once.

---

<!-- problems/required.md -->

# required

**Field error.** A field the DTO needs is missing from the body, or a union's discriminator is
missing.

- **Client:** send the field named by the pointer.
- **Server:** give the constructor parameter a default, or use `Optional`, to make it optional.

---

<!-- problems/unknown-field.md -->

# unknown-field

**Field error.** The body has a field the DTO does not declare. Shirakaba rejects unknown fields so
that typos do not pass silently.

- **Client:** remove the field, or check its spelling (field names are case-sensitive and follow
  the API's names, which may differ from the server's property names).
- **Server:** `#[JsonBody(allowUnknownFields: true)]` accepts and ignores them.

---

<!-- problems/unsupported-media-type.md -->

# unsupported-media-type

**Status 415.** The body's `Content-Type` is not one the endpoint accepts: JSON endpoints take
`application/json` (or any `+json` type), form endpoints `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or
`multipart/form-data`. The `Accept` header of the response names what is accepted where it can.

- **Client:** send the documented media type in `Content-Type`.

---

# API index

Generated by `composer docs:generate`; do not edit. Every public type of every Shirakaba package,
with the first sentence of its documentation. Paths are relative to `vendor/shirakaba/`.

## shirakaba/auth

- `Shirakaba\Auth\Authenticated` (class, `auth/src/Authenticated.php`): Requires an authenticated principal of the parameter's type: `#[Authenticated] User $user`.
- `Shirakaba\Auth\Authentication` (class, `auth/src/Authentication.php`): The principal of the current request, as registered in the RequestScope.
- `Shirakaba\Auth\BearerAuthentication` (class, `auth/src/BearerAuthentication.php`): Verifies `Authorization: Bearer` credentials (RFC 6750, design/09-security.md).
- `Shirakaba\Auth\JwtKey` (class, `auth/src/JwtKey.php`): A verification key bound to exactly one algorithm (design/09-security.md).
- `Shirakaba\Auth\JwtVerifier` (class, `auth/src/JwtVerifier.php`): Shirakaba's minimal JWT (JWS compact) verifier: HS256, RS256 and ES256 (design/09-security.md).
- `Shirakaba\Auth\TokenVerifier` (interface, `auth/src/TokenVerifier.php`): Turns a bearer token into the principal it identifies (design/09-security.md).

## shirakaba/console

- `Shirakaba\Console\Argument` (class, `console/src/Argument.php`): A positional argument: `#[Argument] string $file`.
- `Shirakaba\Console\Console` (class, `console/src/Console.php`): A built console: parses the command line, runs one command and returns its exit code.
- `Shirakaba\Console\ConsoleBuilder` (class, `console/src/ConsoleBuilder.php`): Collects an application's commands (design/10-background-work.md):
- `Shirakaba\Console\Introspection` (class, `console/src/Introspection.php`): Turns descriptions into the text and JSON of the introspection commands.
- `Shirakaba\Console\Option` (class, `console/src/Option.php`): A named option: `#[Option] int $batch = 500` is `--batch=1000` or `--batch 1000`.
- `Shirakaba\Console\Output` (class, `console/src/Output.php`): Where a command writes: standard output for results, standard error for messages.
- `Shirakaba\Console\RouteCommands` (class, `console/src/RouteCommands.php`): Registers `routes` and `routes:show`, so people and coding agents can ask an application which handler serves a request and what it accepts and returns:
- `Shirakaba\Console\Testing\ConsoleResult` (class, `console/src/Testing/ConsoleResult.php`)
- `Shirakaba\Console\Testing\ConsoleTester` (class, `console/src/Testing/ConsoleTester.php`): Runs a console in a test and captures what it writes.
- `Shirakaba\Console\UsageError` (class, `console/src/UsageError.php`): The command line was wrong: an unknown command or option, a missing argument, a value of the wrong type.

- `Shirakaba\Core\Application` (class, `core/src/Application.php`): A built, immutable application: a PSR-15 request handler.

- `Shirakaba\Core\Description\DescribesResponse` (interface, `core/src/Description/DescribesResponse.php`): Implemented by response value classes that can say what they produce without an instance.

- `Shirakaba\Core\Description\FileType` (class, `core/src/Description/FileType.php`): An uploaded file in a multipart body.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Description\ListType` (class, `core/src/Description/ListType.php`)
- `Shirakaba\Core\Description\MapType` (class, `core/src/Description/MapType.php`): An object with arbitrary string keys whose values share one type, such as `{"👍": 2}`.

- `Shirakaba\Core\Description\ObjectType` (class, `core/src/Description/ObjectType.php`): A structured value with named properties, such as a DTO mapped from a JSON object.

- `Shirakaba\Core\Description\UnionType` (class, `core/src/Description/UnionType.php`): One of several object types, told apart by a discriminator property whose value names the member (a tagged union, OpenAPI oneOf with a discriminator).

- `Shirakaba\Core\Observe\Event` (interface, `core/src/Observe/Event.php`): Something a package reports during a request through RequestScope::record(), such as a database statement.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Observe\Observation` (interface, `core/src/Observe/Observation.php`): Events of one request, in order: matched (only when a route matches), handlerFinished (only when the handler returned), failed and cleanupFailed (any number), responseReady (always, last).
- `Shirakaba\Core\Observe\Observer` (interface, `core/src/Observe/Observer.php`): Receives a call for every request and returns the observation that follows it (design/05-errors-and-observability.md).
- `Shirakaba\Core\Observe\RequestSummary` (class, `core/src/Observe/RequestSummary.php`): What observers learn about a request before routing.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Observe\RouteSummary` (class, `core/src/Observe/RouteSummary.php`): The route that matched a request, identified by its template rather than the raw path.
- `Shirakaba\Core\RouteDefinition` (class, `core/src/RouteDefinition.php`): A route being declared.
- `Shirakaba\Core\RouteGroup` (class, `core/src/RouteGroup.php`): Declares routes under a common path prefix and middleware (design/04-routing-and-handlers.md).
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\Cancellation` (class, `core/src/Scope/Cancellation.php`): Cooperative cancellation of one request (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md).
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\Deadline` (class, `core/src/Scope/Deadline.php`): A point in time by which a request should finish, on the monotonic clock (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md).
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\Provide` (class, `core/src/Scope/Provide.php`): Makes application-scoped services available in every request's scope under the types they are asked for (design/08-database.md), for classes built per request such as #[Db] repositories:
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\RequestCancelled` (class, `core/src/Scope/RequestCancelled.php`): Thrown by Cancellation::throwIfRequested().
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\RequestOptions` (class, `core/src/Scope/RequestOptions.php`): What a runtime passes to Application::handleWith() for one request.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\RequestScope` (class, `core/src/Scope/RequestScope.php`): State that belongs to one request (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md): values registered by type, cleanup callbacks, cancellation and an optional deadline.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\ScopeOwningBody` (interface, `core/src/Scope/ScopeOwningBody.php`): A response body that keeps using request resources after the handler returned, and therefore takes over closing the request scope (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md).
- `Shirakaba\Core\Scope\ScopedWork` (class, `core/src/Scope/ScopedWork.php`): Runs work outside HTTP, such as a queued job, with the lifetime and observation of a request (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md and design/05-errors-and-observability.md): a fresh RequestScope whose cleanups run afterwards, and the application's observers seeing it as a "request" with $kind as method and $name as route.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Testing\ResponseJson` (class, `core/src/Testing/ResponseJson.php`): Reads JSON response bodies in tests without hand-written type juggling:
- `Shirakaba\Core\Testing\TestClient` (class, `core/src/Testing/TestClient.php`): Calls an application in-process, without a server or superglobals.
- `Shirakaba\Core\Testing\TestEvent` (class, `core/src/Testing/TestEvent.php`): A recorded event with fixed contents, for testing observers.

## shirakaba/database

- `Shirakaba\Database\Connection` (class, `database/src/Connection.php`): One open connection with its dialect.
- `Shirakaba\Database\ConnectionLeased` (class, `database/src/ConnectionLeased.php`): Reported when a request gets its database connection: a new one, with the time connecting took, or one reused from an earlier request.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Database` (class, `database/src/Database.php`): Application-scoped access to one database (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md).
- `Shirakaba\Database\Dialect\Dialect` (interface, `database/src/Dialect/Dialect.php`): What differs between MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite, in one place.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Dialect\Dialects` (class, `database/src/Dialect/Dialects.php`): Picks the dialect of a connection.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Dialect\MySql` (class, `database/src/Dialect/MySql.php`): MySQL 8.0+ (and compatible servers).
- `Shirakaba\Database\Dialect\PostgreSql` (class, `database/src/Dialect/PostgreSql.php`): PostgreSQL 13+.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Dialect\Sqlite` (class, `database/src/Dialect/Sqlite.php`): SQLite 3.35+ (RETURNING and upserts).
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\ConnectionLost` (class, `database/src/Error/ConnectionLost.php`): The connection to the server failed or was dropped.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\DatabaseError` (class, `database/src/Error/DatabaseError.php`): A database error, wrapping the driver's PDOException.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\ForeignKeyViolation` (class, `database/src/Error/ForeignKeyViolation.php`): A foreign key constraint rejected the statement.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\NotNullViolation` (class, `database/src/Error/NotNullViolation.php`): A NOT NULL column received no value.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\QueryTimedOut` (class, `database/src/Error/QueryTimedOut.php`): A statement ran longer than the time limit of its Reader and was cancelled by the database.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\TransientFailure` (class, `database/src/Error/TransientFailure.php`): A deadlock, serialisation failure or lock timeout; retrying the transaction may succeed.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Error\UniqueViolation` (class, `database/src/Error/UniqueViolation.php`): A unique or primary key constraint rejected the statement.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Lease` (class, `database/src/Lease.php`): A connection borrowed from a Database (design/08-database.md).
- `Shirakaba\Database\Observe\DatabaseEvent` (interface, `database/src/Observe/DatabaseEvent.php`): Something the database packages report while they work, such as a statement, a leased connection or a cache lookup.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Observe\EventSink` (interface, `database/src/Observe/EventSink.php`): Receives the events of one lease or connection (design/08-database.md).
- `Shirakaba\Database\Reader` (class, `database/src/Reader.php`): Read access.
- `Shirakaba\Database\StatementExecuted` (class, `database/src/StatementExecuted.php`): Reported to observers for every statement a request runs.
- `Shirakaba\Database\Testing\TestDatabases` (class, `database/src/Testing/TestDatabases.php`): The databases a test suite can run against: always an in-memory SQLite database, and MySQL and PostgreSQL when SHIRAKABA_TEST_MYSQL_DSN or SHIRAKABA_TEST_PGSQL_DSN are set (with the matching _USER and _PASSWORD variables).
- `Shirakaba\Database\Writer` (class, `database/src/Writer.php`): Read and write access, including transactions.

## shirakaba/database-bridge

- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\DatabaseMiddleware` (class, `database-bridge/src/DatabaseMiddleware.php`): Makes the databases available to #[Db] parameters: the default one, and others by name for `#[Db('analytics')]`.
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\Databases` (class, `database-bridge/src/Databases.php`): The databases of an application by name, for `#[Db('analytics')]` (design/08-database.md).
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\Db` (class, `database-bridge/src/Db.php`): Gives a handler the request's database access (design/08-database.md):
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\EntityCommands` (class, `database-bridge/src/EntityCommands.php`): Registers `entities`, `entities:show` and `entities:check`, so people and coding agents can read how entities map to tables without reading attributes:
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\MigrationCommands` (class, `database-bridge/src/MigrationCommands.php`): Registers the migration commands in a console (design/10-background-work.md), for `shirakaba-migrate` and for an application's own console:
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\RecordedDatabaseEvent` (class, `database-bridge/src/RecordedDatabaseEvent.php`): An event of the database packages as request observers receive it (design/08-database.md).
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\RequestDatabase` (class, `database-bridge/src/RequestDatabase.php`): A request's database access (design/08-database.md): the connection is leased on first use, its events go to the request's observers, and it is released, rolled back and reset when the request scope closes (design/03-runtimes-and-scopes.md and design/08-database.md).
- `Shirakaba\DatabaseBridge\Testing\StatementLog` (class, `database-bridge/src/Testing/StatementLog.php`): Collects the statements of each request, for tests that bound how many a request runs , which catches N+1 queries in any layer:

## shirakaba/docs

- `Shirakaba\Docs\AgentCommands` (class, `docs/src/AgentCommands.php`): Registers agents:sync (design/13-static-analysis-and-agents.md) in a console, for `shirakaba-docs` and an application's own console.
- `Shirakaba\Docs\AgentRules` (class, `docs/src/AgentRules.php`): The block shirakaba-docs agents:sync keeps in a project's AGENTS.md (design/13-static-analysis-and-agents.md).

## shirakaba/form

- `Shirakaba\Form\FileTypes` (class, `form/src/FileTypes.php`): Restricts an uploaded file to media types detected from its content.
- `Shirakaba\Form\FormBody` (class, `form/src/FormBody.php`): Maps an HTML form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data) into a DTO: `#[FormBody] SignUp $input`.
- `Shirakaba\Form\FormList` (class, `form/src/FormList.php`): Declares the item type of a repeated form field (`tags[]=a&tags[]=b`): `#[FormList('string')] array $tags = []`.
- `Shirakaba\Form\MaxFileSize` (class, `form/src/MaxFileSize.php`): Limits the size of an uploaded file, measured on the received data.

## shirakaba/http-client

- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\Addresses` (class, `http-client/src/Addresses.php`): The default address policy: only globally routable addresses (RFC 6890), so a URL from outside cannot reach loopback, private networks, link-local addresses such as cloud metadata endpoints, or other special ranges.
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\CallCancelled` (class, `http-client/src/CallCancelled.php`): The request the client is bound to was cancelled while a call was in flight: a RequestCancelled for the framework, and a ClientExceptionInterface for PSR-18 callers, so sendRequest() throws only what PSR-18 allows.
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\HttpClient` (class, `http-client/src/HttpClient.php`): A PSR-18 client for calling other servers (design/09-security.md), on ext-curl:
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\HttpClientOptions` (class, `http-client/src/HttpClientOptions.php`): Limits and hooks of an HttpClient (design/09-security.md).
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\HttpRequestSent` (class, `http-client/src/HttpRequestSent.php`): Reported to the request's observers for every request the client sends, redirects included.
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\NetworkError` (class, `http-client/src/NetworkError.php`): The exchange failed in transit: connection refused, TLS failure, timeout, or a response larger than the limit ($tooLarge).
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\RequestRefused` (class, `http-client/src/RequestRefused.php`): The client would not send the request: a scheme other than HTTP(S), a host that does not resolve or resolves to a refused address, or too many redirects.
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\Resolver` (interface, `http-client/src/Resolver.php`): Turns a host name into the IP addresses the client may connect to.
- `Shirakaba\HttpClient\SystemResolver` (class, `http-client/src/SystemResolver.php`): Resolves with the system: A and AAAA records from DNS, plus the hosts file.

## shirakaba/http-message

- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\HttpFactory` (class, `http-message/src/HttpFactory.php`): PSR-17 factory for every Shirakaba HTTP message type.
- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\Request` (class, `http-message/src/Request.php`): Immutable PSR-7 client-side (outgoing) request.
- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\Response` (class, `http-message/src/Response.php`): Immutable PSR-7 response.
- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\ServerRequest` (class, `http-message/src/ServerRequest.php`): Immutable PSR-7 server-side (incoming) request.
- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\Stream` (class, `http-message/src/Stream.php`): PSR-7 stream over a PHP stream resource.
- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\UploadedFile` (class, `http-message/src/UploadedFile.php`): PSR-7 uploaded file, backed either by a file path or by a stream.
- `Shirakaba\Http\Message\Uri` (class, `http-message/src/Uri.php`): Immutable PSR-7 URI.

## shirakaba/json

- `Shirakaba\Json\Json` (class, `json/src/Json.php`): A JSON response (design/06-json-and-openapi.md).
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonBody` (class, `json/src/JsonBody.php`): Maps a JSON request body into a DTO: `#[JsonBody] CreateUser $input` (design/06-json-and-openapi.md).
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonBodyFailure` (class, `json/src/JsonBodyFailure.php`): A JSON request body was rejected (design/06-json-and-openapi.md).
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonDto` (class, `json/src/JsonDto.php`): Lets Json encode a class from its constructor fields, the same fields #[JsonResponse] and #[JsonBody] describe, so the declared type and the body cannot drift (design/06-json-and-openapi.md):
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonMapper` (class, `json/src/JsonMapper.php`): Maps JSON text into a DTO with the same rules as #[JsonBody] (design/06-json-and-openapi.md), outside requests: stored JSON columns, messages, files.
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonName` (class, `json/src/JsonName.php`): Names a DTO field differently in JSON, in requests and in described responses: `#[JsonName('per_page')] int $perPage`.
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonResponse` (class, `json/src/JsonResponse.php`): Declares a JSON response of a handler with its body type (design/06-json-and-openapi.md):
- `Shirakaba\Json\JsonUnion` (class, `json/src/JsonUnion.php`): Declares a tagged union of #[JsonDto] classes on the type they share, usually an interface (design/06-json-and-openapi.md):
- `Shirakaba\Json\ListOf` (class, `json/src/ListOf.php`): Declares the item type of an array field in a DTO: `#[ListOf(Tag::class)] array $tags`.
- `Shirakaba\Json\MapOf` (class, `json/src/MapOf.php`): Declares an array field of a DTO as a JSON object with arbitrary keys: `#[MapOf('int')] array $reactions` is `{"👍": 2, "🎉": 1}`.
- `Shirakaba\Json\Optional` (class, `json/src/Optional.php`): A DTO field that may be absent from the request, as distinct from null (design/06-json-and-openapi.md):
- `Shirakaba\Json\OptionalOf` (class, `json/src/OptionalOf.php`): Declares the value type of an Optional DTO field (design/06-json-and-openapi.md).

## shirakaba/log

- `Shirakaba\Log\LoggingObserver` (class, `log/src/LoggingObserver.php`): Writes what the core reports to a PSR-3 logger (design/05-errors-and-observability.md):
- `Shirakaba\Log\StreamLogger` (class, `log/src/StreamLogger.php`): A minimal PSR-3 logger writing one JSON object per line, by default to standard error, which container platforms and FrankenPHP collect.

## shirakaba/mailer

- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Address` (class, `mailer/src/Address.php`): A mail address with an optional display name (design/12-mail-and-templates.md).
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Attachment` (class, `mailer/src/Attachment.php`): A file attached to a mail.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Email` (class, `mailer/src/Email.php`): A mail to send (design/12-mail-and-templates.md): immutable, checked when built, so no field can inject a header.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\EmailSent` (class, `mailer/src/EmailSent.php`): Reported to observers for every mail a transport tried to send (design/12-mail-and-templates.md and design/05-errors-and-observability.md), without addresses, subject or content: the transport, how many recipients, the size, how long it took and, on failure, the kind of error.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\LogMailer` (class, `mailer/src/LogMailer.php`): Writes each mail to a PSR-3 logger instead of sending it, for development.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\MailError` (class, `mailer/src/MailError.php`): A mail could not be sent.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Mailer` (interface, `mailer/src/Mailer.php`): Sends mail (design/12-mail-and-templates.md).
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\MimeWriter` (class, `mailer/src/MimeWriter.php`): Writes an Email as an RFC 5322 message (design/12-mail-and-templates.md): multipart/alternative for text and HTML, multipart/related for inline parts, multipart/mixed for attachments; quoted-printable bodies, base64 attachments, RFC 2047 encoded words for non-ASCII headers, RFC 2231 file names, CRLF line endings and headers folded below 78 characters where possible.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\NullMailer` (class, `mailer/src/NullMailer.php`): Accepts mail and sends nothing, for environments that must not send.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\ObservedMailer` (class, `mailer/src/ObservedMailer.php`): Reports each send to the observers of a request or job as an EmailSent event (design/12-mail-and-templates.md), without addresses or content.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\SentEmail` (class, `mailer/src/SentEmail.php`): What sending a mail produced: its Message-ID (without angle brackets) and the size of the written message in bytes (0 when the mail was only queued).
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\SmtpTransport` (class, `mailer/src/SmtpTransport.php`): Sends mail to an SMTP server (design/12-mail-and-templates.md), one connection per mail:
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Smtp\SmtpConnection` (interface, `mailer/src/Smtp/SmtpConnection.php`): The byte stream SmtpTransport talks over.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Smtp\SocketConnection` (class, `mailer/src/Smtp/SocketConnection.php`): A TCP connection to an SMTP server, with implicit TLS or a later STARTTLS, verified certificates and a timeout on connecting and on every read and write.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\TemplatedEmail` (class, `mailer/src/TemplatedEmail.php`): Builds an Email from three templates (design/12-mail-and-templates.md): `<name>.subject.txt`, `<name>.txt` and an optional `<name>.html`, each looked up in the recipient's locale first.
- `Shirakaba\Mailer\Testing\RecordingMailer` (class, `mailer/src/Testing/RecordingMailer.php`): Keeps sent mail for assertions instead of sending it:

## shirakaba/mailer-queue

- `Shirakaba\MailerQueue\MailJobs` (class, `mailer-queue/src/MailJobs.php`): Registers the handler of SendEmail jobs (design/12-mail-and-templates.md):
- `Shirakaba\MailerQueue\QueuedAddress` (class, `mailer-queue/src/QueuedAddress.php`): An Address as it travels in a SendEmail job.
- `Shirakaba\MailerQueue\QueuedAttachment` (class, `mailer-queue/src/QueuedAttachment.php`): An Attachment as it travels in a SendEmail job, its content in base64.
- `Shirakaba\MailerQueue\QueuedMailer` (class, `mailer-queue/src/QueuedMailer.php`): A Mailer that queues each mail as a SendEmail job in the caller's transaction (design/12-mail-and-templates.md), so the mail leaves only once the data it describes is committed, and is retried when the server answers with a temporary error.
- `Shirakaba\MailerQueue\SendEmail` (class, `mailer-queue/src/SendEmail.php`): The job QueuedMailer pushes: the whole Email as JSON, with the Message-ID fixed when it was queued so a retry can be recognised as the same mail (design/12-mail-and-templates.md).

## shirakaba/migrations

- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Blueprint` (class, `migrations/src/Blueprint.php`): The columns, keys and indexes of a table being created or altered.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Column` (class, `migrations/src/Column.php`): A column being defined in a Blueprint.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\ForeignKey` (class, `migrations/src/ForeignKey.php`): A foreign key being defined.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Index` (class, `migrations/src/Index.php`): An index being defined: on columns or on an expression, with an index method, an operator class and, on PostgreSQL, a statistics target for an expression.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Linter` (class, `migrations/src/Linter.php`): Reports risky changes in migrations before they run:
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Migration` (interface, `migrations/src/Migration.php`): One versioned schema change.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Migrations` (class, `migrations/src/Migrations.php`): An application's migrations, listed in order, with the database they apply to.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Migrator` (class, `migrations/src/Migrator.php`): Applies and rolls back migrations on one connection.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Operation` (class, `migrations/src/Operation.php`): One change a migration makes, as recorded by Schema for linting.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Reversible` (interface, `migrations/src/Reversible.php`): A migration that rollback can undo.
- `Shirakaba\Migrations\Schema` (class, `migrations/src/Schema.php`): Collects the statements of a migration for one dialect.
